$comment: Content for Spectrum (node g32, ages 15-18, Chapter 5): NEW v2 build to GDD 32 (mechanic-embodying), the
identity / orientation / respect node (Thread D · Relationships). "People differ in who they are and who
they love, and every person deserves dignity, respect and safety: that part isn't a debate." 84 researched,
India-grounded, never-explicit scenarios across the-spectrum → myths-and-respect → dignity-for-all → being-you
→ stand-against-bullying → support-and-rights, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (reflect /
branch / strike-rewrite / sort / role-play / match / spot): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: strike-
rewrite (bust the myth kindly), branch (your move), reflect. Built on ONE non-negotiable: respect is a value,
not a debate. Teaches understanding and busts harmful myths WITHOUT disparaging anyone's family or beliefs
separates honest belief-differences (respected) from the dignity floor (always upheld). Supports anyone
questioning, NO pressure to label, complete confidentiality; never outs or infers anyone; sharing is always
the person's own choice. India: consensual same-sex relations decriminalised (2018), NALSA recognised
transgender persons, dignity & equality are constitutional values; framed around settled values, not contested
policy. Routes distress / family-conflict to a trusted adult / counsellor, Tele-MANAS 14416,
Childline 1098. Builds on g7 & g25; links g27 & g31. gameId "spectrum".
title: Spectrum
greet: Hey, I’m Lensy. 🌈 People differ in who they are and who they love, and every person deserves dignity, respect and safety. That isn’t a debate. Let’s explore.

badge.title: Spectrum 🌈
badge.blurb: You understand the spectrum, you can bust harmful myths kindly without disparaging anyone, and you stand for dignity, respect and safety for every person. 🫶

helpLine: Whoever you are and whoever you love, you deserve dignity, respect and safety. Need support? Call Tele-MANAS 14416 or Childline 1098.
reassure: Who you are and who you love is yours, no pressure to label. Struggling or facing conflict at home? Call Tele-MANAS 14416 or Childline 1098. 🫶

scenarios.hook: Lensy: people differ in who they are and who they love, and that's just part of being human. Sit with that.
scenarios.affirm: Human diversity in identity and love is natural and as old as humanity itself.
scenarios.relearn: People vary in who they are and who they love; that's natural human diversity.

scenarios.hook: Match the term to its plain meaning.

pairs.right: Your own sense of your gender
How you treat everyone, no exceptions
What you share is your own choice

scenarios.relearn: Orientation is who you're drawn to; gender identity is your own sense of self; an ally supports dignity.

scenarios.hook: Sort: accurate, respectful language, or not?

items.text: Using the words people use for themselves

scenarios.relearn: Use the words people use for themselves; ask respectfully if unsure.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: this diversity isn't new or foreign, it spans cultures and history, including India's own. Did you know that?
scenarios.affirm: India has its own long-acknowledged traditions of diversity; this is part of human history everywhere.
scenarios.relearn: Diversity in identity spans cultures and history, including India's own traditions.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fact about the spectrum, or a misunderstanding?

items.text: It's existed across all of history
It's part of India's own history

scenarios.relearn: Natural variation across history is fact; 'all the same', 'new fad' or 'foreign import' are misunderstandings.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: understanding isn't about labelling anyone, it's just replacing rumour with calm facts. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Calm, accurate understanding, with no pressure to label anyone, is the whole aim here.
scenarios.relearn: Understanding replaces rumour with facts; it never means labelling anyone.

scenarios.hook: "There are only two ways to be, and everyone fits neatly."

myth.un: Everyone fits neatly into two fixed boxes.
myth.re: Human identity and attraction vary more than two neat boxes allow.
myth.why: Real people are more varied than the stereotype.

scenarios.relearn: Human identity varies more than two neat boxes; that's normal.

scenarios.hook: Match the idea to the plain truth.

pairs.right: It's part of India's own history

scenarios.relearn: Orientation and identity vary, dignity is for everyone, and this diversity is old and Indian too.

scenarios.hook: Sort: respectful curiosity, or crossing a line?
scenarios.relearn: Learning, listening and gentle asking are respectful; demanding, prying and spreading guesses cross a line.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you can understand and respect people without needing to know or decide anything about anyone. See that?
scenarios.affirm: Respect doesn't require knowing anyone's private identity, it's simply how you treat people.
scenarios.relearn: You can respect everyone without needing to know anything private about them.

scenarios.hook: "Talking about this 'creates' more of it."

myth.un: Talking about diversity 'creates' or spreads it.
myth.re: Understanding doesn't create anything; it just replaces fear with facts.
myth.why: People are who they are; information doesn't change that.

scenarios.relearn: Understanding diversity doesn't create it; it replaces fear with facts.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of natural human diversity, or a harmful label?
scenarios.relearn: Variation is natural; 'illness', 'to fix' or 'not natural' are harmful, false labels.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which feels truest, people are varied and that's normal, or everyone must be the same?
scenarios.affirm: Variety is the human norm; expecting everyone to be identical is the myth.
scenarios.relearn: Human variety is normal; expecting everyone to be the same is the myth.

scenarios.hook: Match the respectful move to the moment.

pairs.right: Ask kindly or look it up

scenarios.relearn: Listen, ask kindly, don't pry, decline slurs and respect people even when unsure. That's respect in practice.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: calm, accurate understanding is the foundation for everything else here. Ready to build on it?
scenarios.affirm: With calm understanding in place, respect and dignity follow naturally.
scenarios.relearn: Calm, accurate understanding is the foundation for respect and dignity.

scenarios.hook: "It's just a choice people make."

myth.un: Orientation or identity is just a choice.
myth.re: It isn't a choice; it's part of who someone naturally is.
myth.why: People don't choose who they're drawn to or their sense of self.

scenarios.relearn: Orientation and identity aren't a choice; they're part of who someone is.

scenarios.hook: "It's just a phase they'll grow out of."

myth.un: It's just a phase they'll grow out of.
myth.re: For many it's a lasting part of who they are; it's not yours to time or dismiss.
myth.why: Dismissing it as 'a phase' can be hurtful and isn't for others to decide.

scenarios.relearn: It's not 'just a phase' for others to dismiss; it's part of who they are.

scenarios.hook: "It's a mental illness that needs curing."

myth.un: It's a mental illness that needs curing.
myth.re: It is not a mental illness; health bodies removed it from illness classifications long ago.
myth.why: Calling it an illness is false and causes real harm.

scenarios.relearn: It is not a mental illness; that idea is false and harmful.

scenarios.hook: "It's contagious, being around it spreads it."

myth.un: It's contagious, being around it spreads it.
myth.re: It isn't contagious; people are who they are, and understanding changes nothing about that.
myth.why: Identity isn't caught from others.

scenarios.relearn: Identity isn't contagious; you can't 'catch' who someone is.

scenarios.hook: "It's a foreign, Western import."

myth.un: It's a foreign, Western import.
myth.re: It exists across cultures and history, including India's own long traditions.
myth.why: This diversity is part of human history everywhere, not imported.

scenarios.relearn: It's not a foreign import; it spans cultures and India's own history.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: people can hold different personal beliefs AND still agree everyone deserves safety. Both at once?
scenarios.affirm: Honest differences of belief and a shared floor of dignity for all can coexist, that's the whole approach.
scenarios.relearn: People can differ in belief and still uphold dignity and safety for all.

scenarios.hook: "If you disagree with someone's life, you don't have to be kind to them."

myth.un: Disagreeing means you don't owe someone kindness or safety.
myth.re: You don't have to agree with everyone to treat everyone with dignity and keep them safe.
myth.why: Dignity and safety aren't conditional on agreement.

scenarios.relearn: You can disagree and still owe everyone dignity and safety.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a harmful myth, or an understanding that replaces it?

items.text: "It's a phase to grow out of"

scenarios.relearn: 'Choice', 'illness' and 'phase' are myths; 'part of who someone is' and 'natural variation' are the truth.

scenarios.hook: Sort: respects a person, or disparages them?

items.text: Shaming a person for who they are
Using the words people use for themselves
Throwing a slur to win a point

scenarios.relearn: Correcting kindly, upholding safety and using people's own words respects them; mocking, shaming and slurs disparage.

scenarios.hook: "Caring about this means attacking people's traditions."

myth.un: Standing for dignity means attacking people's traditions.
myth.re: It means upholding a floor of respect and safety for everyone, without disparaging anyone.
myth.why: Dignity for all and respect for people's backgrounds can both be held.

scenarios.relearn: Standing for dignity upholds safety for all without attacking anyone's traditions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the one thing that isn't up for debate is that everyone deserves to be safe. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever anyone believes, everyone's safety and dignity is the non-negotiable floor.
scenarios.relearn: Everyone's dignity and safety is the one thing not up for debate.

scenarios.hook: "People like that don't really deserve respect."

myth.un: 'People like that' don't deserve respect.
myth.re: Every single person deserves dignity, respect and safety, no exceptions.
myth.why: There is no group outside the floor of human dignity.

scenarios.relearn: Every person deserves dignity, respect and safety, no exceptions.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a settled fact, or a discredited claim?
scenarios.relearn: 'Not an illness', 'occurs across history' and 'not catchable' are settled; 'curable', 'modern' and 'spreads' are discredited.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: busting a myth kindly, without putting anyone down, is a real skill. Want to practise it?
scenarios.affirm: Correcting a falsehood while respecting the person is exactly the skill this game builds.
scenarios.relearn: You can correct a myth kindly, without putting anyone down.

scenarios.hook: "Understanding this is dangerous for young people."

myth.un: Understanding diversity is dangerous for young people.
myth.re: Accurate understanding reduces fear, bullying and harm; misinformation is what's dangerous.
myth.why: Knowledge and respect keep young people safer, not less safe.

scenarios.relearn: Accurate understanding reduces harm; misinformation is the real danger.

scenarios.hook: At the tuition centre, your friends start mocking Neel with slurs about who he is.

steps.prompt: They glance at you, waiting for you to laugh. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh along so you don't stand out
options.then: Your laugh makes them louder, and Neel stares at his desk.

options.text: Don't laugh, and say calmly, 'Not okay, guys'
options.then: There's an awkward pause, and one friend stops grinning.

options.text: Say nothing and scroll on your phone
options.then: The mocking goes on, and Neel sees that nobody stopped it.

options.text: Call them idiots, loud enough for the room to hear
options.then: They turn on you, and it becomes a shouting match. Neel shrinks into his seat.

steps.why: A calm 'not okay' sets the line without drama.

steps.prompt: After class, Neel is packing up on his own. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him to ignore them, since they're always like that
options.then: He nods, but he still has to sit near them tomorrow.

options.text: Walk over, say that wasn't okay, and ask if he's alright
options.then: Neel looks up, surprised. "Yeah. Thanks for asking."

options.text: Tell him he should try not to stand out so much
options.then: Neel's face closes. "Right. So it's my fault."

options.text: Leave him be, since he probably wants space
options.then: He walks out alone, head down.

steps.why: Checking on him shows he isn't alone, and that it wasn't his fault.

steps.prompt: The next day, the group plans more 'jokes' about Neel and wants you in. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll come along, but only to watch
options.then: You're there, and your silence looks like agreement.

options.text: Say slurs aren't jokes, and you won't be part of it
options.then: One friend shrugs. "Okay, okay." The plan fizzles out.

options.text: Make an excuse that you're busy that day
options.then: They shrug and carry on without you. Nothing changes for Neel.

options.text: Tell them they're all terrible people for doing it
options.then: They get defensive, and the friend group starts to split.

steps.why: Saying calmly why it's not okay helps the group change.

steps.prompt: A week later, the slurs start again, and someone shoves Neel. What do you do?

options.text: Shove the person back, hard
options.then: It blows up into a fight, and someone could get hurt.

options.text: Film it on your phone to show everyone later
options.then: The video spreads, and Neel is humiliated all over again.

options.text: Stay near Neel and get the tuition teacher right away
options.then: The teacher steps in, and Neel isn't on his own.

options.text: Wait to see if it calms down on its own
options.then: It doesn't, and Neel ends up cornered by the stairs.

steps.why: When it turns physical, support the person and get an adult.

scenarios.debrief: You don't have to make a scene. Not joining, and quietly supporting, counts.
scenarios.relearn: Don't join slurs; calmly decline or support the person.

scenarios.hook: In biology practicals, nobody will partner with Mira because of who she is.

steps.prompt: The teacher says to pair up, and Mira is standing alone again. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for someone else to ask her first
options.then: Nobody does, and the teacher has to assign her a partner.

options.text: Ask Mira to pair up, and make room at your bench
options.then: Mira's face relaxes, and she pulls up a stool.

options.text: Ask the teacher to tell the class to include her
options.then: The teacher announces it, and Mira looks mortified.

options.text: Stay with your usual partner, but smile at Mira
options.then: She smiles back faintly, then works alone.

steps.why: A simple, warm invitation includes her with no fuss.

steps.prompt: Next practical, your usual partner whispers that anyone who works with Mira will get talked about. What do you say?

options.text: Say 'Let them talk. She's good at this.'
options.then: Your partner shrugs, and the whisper goes nowhere.

options.text: Say people only work with her out of pity
options.then: Mira overhears, and her shoulders drop.

options.text: Agree, and say you'll keep your distance too
options.then: Your partner nods. Mira works alone again.

options.text: Tell your partner off loudly in front of the class
options.then: Heads turn, and Mira shrinks in her seat.

steps.why: Treating it as normal makes including her normal for everyone.

steps.prompt: At lunch, Mira is sitting alone again. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with her for a bit, then go back to your group
options.then: She smiles, but when you leave she's alone again.

options.text: Ask if she'd like to join your group's table
options.then: She hesitates, then brings her tiffin over. The talk turns to exams.

options.text: Tell your group they have to be nice to her now
options.then: They agree, but it feels like a chore to them, and she can tell.

options.text: Leave her be, assuming she likes eating alone
options.then: Mira eats quickly and leaves early.

steps.why: Bringing her into everyday group life is real belonging.

scenarios.debrief: Quiet inclusion is one of the most powerful forms of respect.
scenarios.relearn: Including someone warmly is everyday dignity in action.

scenarios.hook: You're still unsure what you think about all this, when Dev in your class starts getting bullied for who he is.

steps.prompt: Some boys block Dev's way in the corridor and jeer at him. What do you do?

options.text: Stay out of it, since you haven't made up your mind
options.then: The jeering goes on, and Dev has to push past alone.

options.text: Fetch a teacher right away, then come back to Dev
options.then: The teacher walks over, and the boys scatter.

options.text: Push into the group and tell them to back off
options.then: One boy shoves you, and it nearly turns into a fight.

options.text: Message a friend about what's happening
options.then: Your friend replies 'omg', and nothing changes for Dev.

steps.why: Safety doesn't depend on your views, and getting an adult keeps everyone safer.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend says there's no point helping Dev if you don't 'agree with' him. What do you say?

options.text: Say you don't need to agree with someone to keep them safe
options.then: Your friend pauses. "Huh. Fair enough."

options.text: Say you'd only step in to stay out of trouble
options.then: Your friend nods, and the real point is lost.

options.text: Call your friend a bigot and walk off
options.then: Your friend gets defensive, and the talk ends there.

options.text: Agree that it's probably best not to get involved
options.then: Your friend smirks, and next time it'll feel harder to help.

steps.why: The dignity floor is for everyone, whatever your views.

steps.prompt: The next day, Dev sits alone in the canteen, looking down. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with him, and say no one deserves what happened
options.then: Dev looks up. "Thanks. That means a lot."

options.text: Tell him you're still not sure about people like him, but sorry
options.then: Dev's face closes. "Oh. Okay."

options.text: Wave from across the room, then sit with your friends
options.then: Dev waves back, but stays on his own.

options.text: Tell him to keep a lower profile so it doesn't happen again
options.then: Dev looks down. "So it's on me."

steps.why: Respect without conditions tells him the problem was never him.

steps.prompt: A week later, the same boys start following Dev home. What do you do?

options.text: Tell Dev to take a different route and keep quiet about it
options.then: He changes his route, but he's scared every day.

options.text: Walk with Dev, and help him tell a teacher or his parents
options.then: The teacher calls the boys in, and Dev feels safer walking home.

options.text: Wait with friends to teach the boys a lesson
options.then: It turns into a scuffle, and two people get hurt.

options.text: Tell yourself it's not your business, since you're still unsure
options.then: Dev walks home alone, looking over his shoulder.

steps.why: Ongoing targeting needs an adult. Your views don't change that.

scenarios.debrief: Dignity and safety don't depend on agreeing about everything.
scenarios.relearn: You can keep someone safe while working out your own views.

scenarios.hook: While your group waits for the bus, Kunal drops a slur about a classmate.
scenarios.setup: A couple of people laugh, and Kunal looks at you.

steps.prompt: Kunal grins and says: "What? It's just a word. Everyone says it."

options.text: "Haha, you're too much, man."
options.then: Kunal laughs. "See? Even you think it's funny."

options.text: "Let's not use that word. It's not okay."
options.then: Kunal pauses. "Okay, okay. It's not that deep, though."

options.text: "That's disgusting. What is wrong with you?"
options.then: His face hardens. "Relax. Why are you making it a whole thing?"

options.text: "Not in front of me, at least. Save it."
options.then: Kunal shrugs. "Fine. I'll save it for later, then."

steps.why: A short, calm line names the harm without turning it into a fight.

steps.prompt: On the bus, Kunal says: "Honestly, people get offended by everything these days."

options.text: "True. Everyone's so touchy now."
options.then: "Exactly," Kunal says, and leans back, satisfied.

options.text: "Only people like you would say that."
options.then: "People like me? Wow," he says, and turns to the window.

options.text: "It's not about offence. That word puts people down."
options.then: Kunal is quiet for a moment. "I never thought of it like that."

options.text: "Can we just drop it and talk about the match instead?"
options.then: "Sure," he says. The word hangs there, unexplained.

steps.why: Explaining why, once and calmly, gives him a reason to change, not just a rule.

steps.prompt: Next day in the canteen, Kunal starts the word out of habit. Priya frowns, and he asks you: "We can still say stuff, right?"

options.text: "Say what you want. I'm not your teacher."
options.then: He finishes the word, and the table laughs again.

options.text: "Just don't say it near them. They might hear you."
options.then: Kunal nods. "Fair. I'll check who's around first."

options.text: "If you don't get it, why are we even friends?"
options.then: Kunal looks stung. "Wow. Over one word?"

options.text: "Say plenty. Just not words that put people down."
options.then: He laughs. "Okay. That's a fair deal."

steps.why: It draws a clear line on slurs without shaming him as a person.

scenarios.relearn: A calm 'let's not use that word' upholds dignity without drama.

scenarios.hook: At break, your friend Ritu overhears two classmates making cruel comments about her.
scenarios.setup: Later she sits beside you, eyes red.

steps.prompt: Ritu asks quietly: "Did you hear what they said about me?"

options.text: "Just ignore it. They're not worth your time."
options.then: Ritu nods, but she goes quiet. "Easy to say."

options.text: "Want me to go and sort them out right now?"
options.then: Ritu grabs your arm. "No! That'll make it worse."

options.text: "I did. That was wrong of them. You deserve respect."
options.then: Ritu lets out a breath. "I thought maybe I was overreacting."

options.text: "Maybe they didn't mean it the way it sounded."
options.then: Ritu looks away. "They meant it."

steps.why: Naming it as wrong, and her as deserving respect, tells her she isn't the problem.

steps.prompt: Ritu asks: "Is it something about me? Should I change how I am?"

options.text: "No. Nothing about you needs fixing. They were wrong."
options.then: Ritu nods slowly. "I needed to hear that from someone."

options.text: "Maybe keep a lower profile till it dies down."
options.then: Her shoulders drop. "So I should just hide."

options.text: "Everyone gets teased. It toughens you up in the end."
options.then: "It doesn't feel like it's making me stronger," she says.

options.text: "Don't think about it. Come on. Let's go get chai."
options.then: Ritu manages a smile, but the question stays in her eyes.

steps.why: Being herself never earns cruelty. The problem is the comments, not her.

steps.prompt: Ritu asks: "What if they keep doing it tomorrow?"

options.text: "Then you snap back at them, hard."
options.then: "I'm not like that," she says. "I'd just freeze."

options.text: "Then we keep well away from them, I guess."
options.then: "Maybe. But they're in every one of my classes."

options.text: "Then I'll post about what they did, so everyone knows."
options.then: "Please don't. I don't want more people talking."

options.text: "Then I'm with you, and we tell Fernandes ma'am."
options.then: Ritu nods. "Okay. If you come with me, I can do that."

steps.why: Staying with her and bringing in a trusted teacher means she isn't facing it alone.

scenarios.relearn: Affirming someone's right to respect helps after they're hurt.

scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 moves that put the person at risk, not the safe ally moves.

scene.text: Sitting with someone who's excluded
A dramatic scene that turns the crowd on them
Calmly declining to join mockery
Posting 'I'm defending them' so all now know who
Quietly telling a teacher they need help

scenarios.why: A dramatic scene and an exposing post can endanger them; quiet support, declining and an adult are safe.
scenarios.relearn: Quiet, steady allyship, sitting with someone, declining mockery, is the safe kind.

scenarios.hook: At a sleepover, the gossip starts, and you're tempted to share a guess about your classmate Kiran.

steps.prompt: Everyone leans in, waiting for something juicy. What do you do?

options.text: Share it, but say it's 'just a guess'
options.then: Within minutes, the guess is being repeated as fact.

options.text: Keep the guess to yourself. It's not yours to share
options.then: The gossip moves on to someone's new haircut.

options.text: Hint at it so no one can say you told
options.then: Your friends fill in the blanks, and Kiran's name comes up.

options.text: Ask if anyone else has noticed anything about Kiran
options.then: Everyone starts guessing out loud.

steps.why: A person's identity is theirs alone to share. It's never gossip.

steps.prompt: Later that night, a friend leans in: 'Honestly, everyone suspects Kiran.' What do you say?

options.text: Say guessing about Kiran isn't fair, and change the topic
options.then: A couple of friends nod, and the chat moves on.

options.text: Say you suspect it too, but won't say more
options.then: That's enough. Your friend repeats it to someone by Monday.

options.text: Say it's fine to talk, since Kiran isn't here
options.then: The guesses get more personal.

options.text: Tell your friend she's a horrible person for saying it
options.then: She goes quiet and hurt, and the sleepover turns awkward.

steps.why: Refusing to guess protects Kiran's privacy and safety.

steps.prompt: On Monday, a classmate passes the Kiran gossip on to you. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Kiran directly whether the rumour is true
options.then: Kiran goes pale. "Who's saying that?"

options.text: Stay quiet, since it's already out there anyway
options.then: The rumour keeps travelling, a little bigger each time.

options.text: Shut it down: 'Not ours to talk about'
options.then: The classmate shrugs and stops. One less place for it to spread.

options.text: Tell Kiran exactly who started it, so she knows
options.then: Kiran is shaken, and a fight starts brewing.

steps.why: Stopping it with you limits the harm, without prying into Kiran's life.

scenarios.debrief: Whether, when and to whom anyone shares anything is only ever their own choice.
scenarios.relearn: Never out anyone; a person's identity is theirs alone to share.

scenarios.hook: In a class discussion, Farhan uses respectful words for people of every identity, and some classmates laugh.

steps.prompt: A few people snigger and mimic how he said it. What do you do?

options.text: Back him up: 'That's just the normal, decent way to say it'
options.then: The sniggering trails off, and Farhan sits up a little.

options.text: Laugh along with the others
options.then: Farhan goes quiet for the rest of the class.

options.text: Stay quiet, then tell Farhan after class that you agreed
options.then: He smiles, but in the moment he stood alone.

options.text: Tell the class loudly that they're all ignorant
options.then: People roll their eyes, and the discussion turns into an argument.

steps.why: Backing respectful words out loud makes respect the group's normal.

steps.prompt: At break, a classmate asks why the words even matter. What do you say?

options.text: Say they don't, really. It's just a trend
options.then: He nods, and the mocking feels fine to him now.

options.text: Say words can make people feel respected or mocked
options.then: He thinks. "Huh. Never thought of it like that."

options.text: Say teachers will mark you down if you don't use them
options.then: He shrugs. "So it's just about rules."

options.text: Tell him he should already know that
options.then: He gets defensive and stops listening.

steps.why: Explaining that words carry respect helps people choose them.

steps.prompt: Next class, someone uses an old insulting label as a 'joke'. What do you do?

options.text: Let it slide this time, since it's only a joke
options.then: The joke spreads, and the old label is back in the group.

options.text: Call them out by name in the class group chat
options.then: It turns into a public argument, and the point gets lost.

options.text: Say plainly, 'Let's use the words people use for themselves'
options.then: There's a pause, and a few people nod.

options.text: Look at Farhan, hoping he'll say something
options.then: Farhan has to speak up again, alone.

steps.why: Using people's own words is basic decency, and saying so sets the norm.

scenarios.debrief: Treating respect as normal, not mockable, shifts the whole group.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: there's nothing you need to 'admit' or 'confess'. You've done nothing wrong. Hear it?
scenarios.affirm: This isn't a secret to confess; being who you are is not a wrong, so there's nothing to admit.
scenarios.relearn: There's nothing to 'admit' or 'confess'; you've done nothing wrong.

scenarios.hook: A quiz app in your feed promises to 'tell you what you really are' in ten questions.

steps.prompt: Your friend Meher sends it too, saying it's scarily accurate. What do you do?

options.text: Take it, and treat the result as the final word
options.then: It gives you a label in big letters, and you feel boxed in.

options.text: Skip it. No app gets to define who you are
options.then: You close the tab. The question stays yours, to explore in your own time.

options.text: Take it again and again until the answer feels right
options.then: Each try says something different, and you end up more confused.

options.text: Take it for fun, then post your result in the group
options.then: The group starts debating your result, and you wish you hadn't posted.

steps.why: Understanding yourself is yours to do, at your pace. A quiz can't do it for you.

steps.prompt: A week later, the same quiz keeps popping up in your feed: 'Find out who you really are today!' What do you do?

options.text: Tap it, just to see what it says
options.then: It gives you a result, and the doubt creeps in.

options.text: Pay for the 'full report' it keeps advertising
options.then: The report eats your pocket money and says nothing you can trust.

options.text: Hide the ad and tell your feed to stop showing it
options.then: Your feed goes quiet, and the question feels less urgent.

options.text: Let it keep showing, and promise yourself you'll ignore it
options.then: The ads keep coming, and each one tugs at you a little.

steps.why: Stepping away from what pressures you protects your own pace.

steps.prompt: Later, Meher asks how anyone could understand themselves better, if not through quizzes. What do you say?

options.text: Finding the one test out there that's actually accurate
options.then: Meher shrugs. "Is there even such a thing?"

options.text: Letting close friends decide what label fits them
options.then: Meher laughs nervously. "That's a lot of power to give us."

options.text: Time, good info and talking to someone they trust
options.then: Meher nods slowly. "That sounds way better than a quiz."

options.text: Setting a deadline to have it all worked out
options.then: Meher raises an eyebrow. "Why the rush?"

steps.why: There's no test or deadline. Time, good info and trusted people help most.

scenarios.debrief: No app, quiz or label gets the final word on who you are. Only you do.
scenarios.relearn: No quiz or app defines you; understanding yourself is yours alone.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Tanmay keeps pushing you to say what you 'are', and won't let it drop.

steps.prompt: He brings it up again on the walk home. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're still working things out, and ask him to respect that
options.then: Tanmay pauses. "Okay, okay," he says, though he still looks curious.

options.text: Say you're still working things out, then ask what he thinks you are
options.then: Tanmay starts guessing, and now his guesses ring in your ears.

options.text: Snap that he's the worst friend ever
options.then: Tanmay goes red and walks off, and the walk home ends in silence.

options.text: Wonder if a best friend has a right to know
options.then: The thought nags at you all evening, though nobody is owed this.

steps.why: A calm boundary is enough. You don't owe anyone an answer about yourself.

steps.prompt: The next day, Tanmay jokes about it in front of two classmates. What do you do?

options.text: Get even with a joke about his crush
options.then: Everyone laughs at him now, and he looks hurt and angry.

options.text: Tell yourself it's your fault for seeming unsure
options.then: Your face burns, as if you'd done something wrong.

options.text: Ask him plainly to drop it
options.then: Tanmay blinks. "Sorry, sorry." The classmates move on to cricket scores.

options.text: Ask the classmates to take your side against him
options.then: One shrugs, one smirks, and now three people are in your business.

steps.why: Asking plainly is enough. Being teased about this is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, the questions start again, now in late-night texts. What do you do?

options.text: Ask another friend to tell Tanmay off for you
options.then: Your friend gets heated, and now there are two arguments instead of one.

options.text: Talk it over with a trusted adult, like the school counsellor
options.then: The counsellor helps you plan what to say, and you feel less alone with it.

options.text: Screenshot his texts and post them to shame him
options.then: His friends hit back, and the whole class is talking about you two.

options.text: Tell yourself a real friend would just give him an answer
options.then: You start to feel you're the problem, though you're not.

steps.why: When pressure keeps going, a trusted adult can help. It's not on you alone.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Tanmay apologises and asks how to make it right. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's fine and that it never really bothered you
options.then: He relaxes, and never learns how much it hurt.

options.text: Accept, and tell him honestly that the questions hurt
options.then: Tanmay nods. "I didn't think about how it felt. I'm sorry."

options.text: Say he can make up for it by sharing his own secrets
options.then: He looks uneasy. Now the pressure has just switched sides.

options.text: Accept, then tease him about it for weeks
options.then: He laughs at first, then starts keeping his distance.

steps.why: Honest words help him understand, and give the friendship a real fresh start.

scenarios.debrief: You can set a kind boundary. No one is owed a label from you, and the pressure is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: You can ask others to respect that you're still working things out.

scenarios.hook: A post online said you 'have to' know who you are by now, and it's stuck in your head.

steps.prompt: It's midnight, and the post is still on your mind. What do you do?

options.text: Stay up until you've decided, once and for all
options.then: By 3 a.m. you're exhausted and no clearer than before.

options.text: Read the comments to see what everyone else has decided
options.then: Everyone sounds so sure, and you feel further behind.

options.text: Comment asking strangers to decide for you
options.then: Confident replies pour in about a person they've never met.

options.text: Remind yourself there's no deadline, and put the phone down
options.then: You breathe out. The urgency fades as the screen goes dark.

steps.why: There's no deadline. A forced answer under pressure rarely brings real calm.

steps.prompt: The next day, the same account posts: 'Unsure means you're in denial.' What do you think?

options.text: Unsure is a normal place to be, for as long as it takes
options.then: The post loses some of its grip on you.

options.text: Maybe I'm in denial and should admit something
options.then: You feel cornered by a stranger's words.

options.text: I'll argue in the comments until they back down
options.then: Your comment draws dozens of replies, and the post gets even more reach.

options.text: I'll follow them, just to keep track of what they say
options.then: Their posts keep landing in your feed, each with a new deadline.

steps.why: Being unsure is okay. It isn't denial, and it isn't a problem to fix.

steps.prompt: A week later, your feed is full of posts like that. What do you do?

options.text: Keep scrolling, hoping one finally gives you the answer
options.then: Every post says something different, and you feel more lost.

options.text: Mute them, but check their pages now and then
options.then: Each visit pulls the pressure right back in.

options.text: Mute those accounts and follow calmer, accurate sources
options.then: Your feed feels lighter, and you can think at your own pace.

options.text: Tell yourself the feed must know something you don't
options.then: You start trusting the algorithm more than yourself.

steps.why: You choose what feeds your mind. Calm, accurate sources help more than pressure.

scenarios.debrief: Online urgency isn't your timeline. You decide nothing on anyone's clock.
scenarios.relearn: There's no rush online or off; you set your own pace.

scenarios.hook: You've felt low about all this for a while, and it's getting heavy to carry alone.

steps.prompt: After class, Mrs Fernandes asks if everything's okay. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it's not serious enough for a teacher's time
options.then: She says her door is open anyway, and you walk off still carrying it.

options.text: Say things have been heavy, and ask if you could talk sometime
options.then: She nods. "Of course. Come by at lunch tomorrow, just us."

options.text: Tell her everything, right there in the busy school corridor
options.then: Classmates walk past mid-sentence, and you feel exposed.

options.text: Say you'll handle it yourself, since asking is weak
options.then: She says she's there if you change your mind. The weight stays.

steps.why: Saying it's been heavy opens the door. Asking for help is strength, not weakness.

steps.prompt: That weekend, the heaviness comes back hard, and school feels far away. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself you've already used up your chance at help
options.then: You sit with it alone, though help hasn't gone anywhere.

options.text: Play games all night to block it out
options.then: The hours pass, but the heaviness is still there when you stop.

options.text: Call Tele-MANAS 14416 to talk to someone now
options.then: The person on the line listens, and you feel steadier by the end.

options.text: Decide helplines are only for real emergencies
options.then: You don't call, and the night stretches out long and heavy.

steps.why: Help is there between school days too. Tele-MANAS 14416 is a call away.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, you're feeling a bit lighter. What helps keep it that way?

options.text: Make regular time to talk with a trusted adult
options.then: Those talks become a steady part of your week.

options.text: Stop reaching out now, since you feel a lot better
options.then: A hard week comes, and you're not sure who to turn to.

options.text: Tell yourself you were being dramatic before
options.then: You start doubting what you felt, and reaching out gets harder.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll never feel low again
options.then: When a low day comes, it feels like you've failed.

steps.why: Support works best as a steady habit, not only for emergencies.

scenarios.debrief: When it gets heavy, confidential, caring support is always within reach.
scenarios.relearn: If it gets heavy, reach a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Rohit hints he might 'tell people' something about you that you haven't shared.

steps.prompt: He says it again, smirking, as you pack your bag. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: I must have done something to deserve this
options.then: Shame floods in, though the threat is entirely on him.

options.text: This is on him, and I don't have to face it alone
options.then: Your hands still shake, but your head feels clearer.

options.text: He's probably joking, so it doesn't really count
options.then: You laugh it off in your head, but your stomach stays tight.

options.text: Maybe I should tell everyone first, before he can
options.then: The thought of doing it on his terms makes your stomach drop.

steps.why: A threat to out someone is never their fault. You don't have to carry it alone.

steps.prompt: That evening he messages: 'Do my project or everyone finds out.' What do you do?

options.text: Screenshot it and plan to show a trusted adult tomorrow
options.then: Saving it feels steadier. Now there's proof, and a plan.

options.text: Threaten to spread rumours about him back
options.then: He gets angrier, and his next message is worse.

options.text: Post his message publicly to expose him
options.then: People start asking what he meant, and the guessing begins.

options.text: Ask your friends to gang up on him at school
options.then: Your friends are up for it, and you realise someone could get hurt.

steps.why: Saving proof and telling a trusted adult gets you real backup.

steps.prompt: The next morning, you think about who could help. Who do you go to?

options.text: The school counsellor, who can handle it carefully
options.then: She listens, says it's not your fault, and makes a plan to keep you safe.

options.text: Rohit's best friend, to get him to back off
options.then: The friend shrugs, then tells Rohit you came to him.

options.text: Your class group chat, to warn everyone about him
options.then: The chat explodes with guesses about what he meant.

options.text: Your class teacher, in front of the whole class
options.then: Your teacher kindly asks to talk after class, but everyone has already turned to stare.

steps.why: A counsellor can act carefully and privately, so your story stays yours.

steps.prompt: A week later, Rohit has gone quiet, but you still feel shaky. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself it's over, so the feelings don't count
options.then: The worry stays, but now you feel you shouldn't have it.

options.text: Dig up Rohit's secrets in case you need them
options.then: You spend hours on it and feel worse, not safer.

options.text: Talk to an adult you trust, and save Childline 1098
options.then: Knowing who to turn to helps the shakiness ease, bit by bit.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll never trust anyone with anything again
options.then: You feel safer for a moment, then very alone.

steps.why: Feelings can last after a threat stops. Support, and Childline 1098, are there.

scenarios.debrief: Your story is yours. A threat to out you is never your fault, and a trusted adult can help.
scenarios.relearn: What's yours to share is yours; get a trusted adult if someone threatens to out you.

scenarios.hook: You want to read up on all this, but worry someone at home will see your search history.

steps.prompt: You're home alone with the family laptop. What do you do?

options.text: Decide that even wanting to know is something to hide
options.then: The questions stay, now with a layer of shame on top.

options.text: Read a few accurate sources privately, at your own pace
options.then: You close the laptop calmer, knowing a little more.

options.text: Click whatever pops up first, even angry forums
options.then: A forum full of cruel comments leaves you shaken.

options.text: Ask in a public comment section, under your real name
options.then: Strangers reply, and a classmate likes your comment.

steps.why: Learning accurate facts, privately and at your own pace, is yours to do.

steps.prompt: The next day, a classmate says looking this stuff up 'means something' about a person. What do you think?

options.text: Wanting to learn means being curious, nothing more
options.then: His comment loses its sting.

options.text: Maybe I should stop reading so no one wonders
options.then: You shut the curiosity down, and the questions don't go anywhere.

options.text: I need to work out what it 'means' before anyone else does
options.then: The pressure to decide creeps back in.

options.text: I'll ask him what he thinks it means
options.then: He shrugs and starts guessing about people in your class.

steps.why: Wanting to understand is just curiosity. It doesn't say anything about anyone.

steps.prompt: A week on, you have more questions than answers. Where do you turn next?

options.text: A popular influencer's DMs
options.then: The influencer never replies, but a stranger in the comments messages you instead.

options.text: The school counsellor, to talk it through calmly
options.then: She answers with care and says there's no rush to work anything out.

options.text: Endless searching for one site with every answer
options.then: Each site says something different, and you're up past midnight.

options.text: A relative who loves gossip but seems open-minded
options.then: She's kind, but by the weekend your cousins are asking questions.

steps.why: A trusted adult like a counsellor can answer questions calmly and with care.

scenarios.debrief: Quietly learning the facts is yours to do, privately and pressure-free.
scenarios.relearn: You can learn about yourself privately, at your own pace.

scenarios.hook: At a cousin's engagement, Bua says you should 'just pick' so the family knows what to call you.

steps.prompt: She says it loudly, and a few relatives turn to look. What do you do?

options.text: Argue with her until she admits she's wrong
options.then: Voices rise, and the whole function turns to watch.

options.text: Say gently you're not ready to label anything
options.then: Bua blinks. "Hmm. Okay, beta." Someone passes round more sweets.

options.text: Tell yourself it's your fault for confusing the family
options.then: Your cheeks burn, though there's nothing to be sorry for.

options.text: Tell yourself you owe everyone an answer right now
options.then: Your mind races for an answer you don't have, and the moment drags on.

steps.why: A calm 'I'm not ready, and that's okay' holds your pace without a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, Bua catches you near the buffet and says it's 'for your own good'. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat that you'll share if and when you're ready
options.then: Bua sighs, but she pats your arm and lets it go.

options.text: Believe her, since elders know what's best for you
options.then: Her words follow you round the function all evening.

options.text: Tell her she's rude and old-fashioned
options.then: Bua looks hurt, and your mother hears about it within minutes.

options.text: Ask your mother to tell Bua off in front of everyone
options.then: Your mother is caught off guard, and an argument starts by the gate.

steps.why: Repeating your boundary calmly is enough. You owe no one a label on their schedule.

steps.prompt: On the drive home, the whole thing keeps replaying in your head. What do you do?

options.text: Decide something must be wrong with you, since everyone's confused
options.then: You feel heavier, though being unsure is completely okay.

options.text: Tell yourself family pressure is just how it has to be
options.then: You feel stuck, as if you have no say in your own life.

options.text: Talk it over with an adult you trust, like a favourite teacher
options.then: Talking it through, you feel less alone, and you plan what to say next time.

options.text: Post a vague, angry status about 'nosy relatives'
options.then: Bua sees it, and the family group chat goes quiet and tense.

steps.why: Talking to an adult you trust helps with family pressure. And it's not your fault.

steps.prompt: At the next family function, Bua starts to raise it again. What do you do?

options.text: Smile and say 'Still no rush, Bua' and stay near someone kind
options.then: She laughs and drops it. Your cousin gives your arm a squeeze.

options.text: Lecture her in front of everyone about respect
options.then: The room goes stiff, and the evening becomes about the argument.

options.text: Ask her what she would pick for you
options.then: She names a label with a laugh, and it sticks in your head for days.

options.text: Tell her she'll be the last person you ever tell anything
options.then: Bua's face falls, and other relatives tut at you.

steps.why: A light, steady boundary and a supportive person nearby make each time easier.

scenarios.debrief: No one's need for a label outranks your right to take your time, and the pressure is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: You can decline to label yourself for others' convenience.

scenarios.hook: A video says posting about who you are online is 'the only way to be free', and you feel tempted.

steps.prompt: Your thumb hovers over the post button. What do you do?

options.text: Post it now, to prove you're not hiding
options.then: Within minutes, people you barely know are commenting, and you can't take it back.

options.text: Pause. Sharing is your choice, in your time
options.then: You save it as a draft. Nothing is lost by waiting.

options.text: Post it, and delete it in an hour if it feels wrong
options.then: Someone screenshots it in the first ten minutes.

options.text: Post it to a 'close friends' list you haven't checked in months
options.then: Later you notice the list includes an old tuition group.

steps.why: A public post can't be undone. Sharing is yours to choose, if and when you want.

steps.prompt: The next day, the creator posts: 'If you're not out, you're living a lie.' What do you think?

options.text: Maybe keeping anything private makes me fake
options.then: Guilt settles in, though privacy is your right.

options.text: I'll argue in the comments until they apologise
options.then: Your comment draws a pile of replies, and your name is out there now.

options.text: My timing is mine. Privacy isn't a lie
options.then: The creator's words lose some of their pull.

options.text: Maybe the creator knows my life better than I do
options.then: You start letting a stranger's video set your pace.

steps.why: Privacy is not a lie. No creator gets to set your timeline.

steps.prompt: A month later, you're thinking about who you'd want to talk to about all this. What feels right?

options.text: Whoever asks first, so it's out of the way
options.then: The thought alone makes your chest tight.

options.text: Letting a friend do the talking for me
options.then: Your friend agrees, but now you can't control who hears what.

options.text: Waiting until the creator says the time is right for me
options.then: You keep checking their page for a sign that never comes.

options.text: Taking my time, and maybe one trusted person, if I want
options.then: The choice feels like yours again, with no clock on it.

steps.why: Whether, when and who you tell is yours. One trusted person, at your pace, is one way.

scenarios.debrief: Whether, when and to whom you share is yours alone. No video decides it.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing is your choice, in your time, with people you trust.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Ishaan, who confided in you last week, begs you to 'figure out' a label for him.

steps.prompt: He looks exhausted and keeps saying he just wants to know. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest a label so he can feel sorted
options.then: He nods, but over the next days he seems less sure, not more.

options.text: Tell him there's no rush, and he's okay without a label
options.then: Ishaan's shoulders drop. "Really? I thought I had to know by now."

options.text: Say you'll research it tonight and get back to him
options.then: He waits for your verdict, as if it's yours to decide.

options.text: Tell him to stop overthinking, and it'll sort itself out
options.then: Ishaan goes quiet. "Okay. Sorry I brought it up."

steps.why: He doesn't need a label to be okay. Easing the pressure helps most.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Ishaan says he still feels lost about it all. What do you do?

options.text: Listen, and ask what would help him right now
options.then: He thinks, then says, "Maybe just talking. Like this."

options.text: Send him a long list of articles to read tonight
options.then: He thanks you, but he looks overwhelmed by the list.

options.text: Tell him what you'd do if you were him
options.then: He starts measuring himself against your answer.

options.text: Bring in another friend to help him decide
options.then: Ishaan freezes. He hadn't told anyone else.

steps.why: Asking what he needs keeps him in charge of his own journey.

steps.prompt: Later that week, Ishaan admits he's been feeling really low for a while. What do you do?

options.text: Promise to keep it all a secret, whatever happens next
options.then: He relaxes, but you're left holding a worry you can't share.

options.text: Tell him everyone feels low, and it'll pass
options.then: He nods, but his eyes stay on the floor.

options.text: Stay with him, and suggest the counsellor or Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: He agrees to see the counsellor, if you'll walk there with him.

options.text: Tell his parents everything he's told you, to get him help
options.then: Ishaan goes pale when he finds out what you shared.

steps.why: Staying with him and pointing to real support helps, without outing him.

scenarios.debrief: Helping a friend means easing the pressure, not adding a label.
scenarios.relearn: A confiding friend needs reassurance, not a label you assign them.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Gurpreet has just shared something about who she is, and now she's watching your face.
scenarios.setup: You're sitting on the steps outside tuition.

steps.prompt: Gurpreet asks: "Do you still see me the same way?"

options.text: "Hmm. Let me think about whether it changes things."
options.then: Gurpreet's smile drops. "Oh. Okay."

options.text: "Of course. You're my friend. Nothing changes."
options.then: She laughs shakily. "I practised this for weeks."

options.text: "Totally. Just don't make it your whole personality."
options.then: She flinches. "I wasn't planning to."

options.text: "Of course. I mean, I sort of knew already."
options.then: Gurpreet goes still. "Was it that obvious? I wanted to tell you myself."

steps.why: Simple, unchanged warmth is the answer she was hoping for.

steps.prompt: After a quiet moment, Gurpreet asks: "Are we still on for badminton on Sunday?"

options.text: "Sure, but maybe just us, not the whole group."
options.then: Gurpreet hesitates. "Oh. So you'd rather people didn't see us together."

options.text: "Maybe give me a couple of weeks first."
options.then: Her face falls. "Right. Take your time."

options.text: "Yes, and I'll tell the others so it's not awkward."
options.then: She freezes. "Tell them what? I didn't say you could."

options.text: "Obviously. I've already booked the court."
options.then: She grins. "Okay. Normal Sunday, then."

steps.why: Keeping your plans just as they were shows nothing has changed.

steps.prompt: Gurpreet picks at her shoelace and says: "I'm scared of how other people will react."

options.text: "That's fair. Whatever happens, I'm with you."
options.then: She leans into your shoulder. "That helps. A lot."

options.text: "They'll be fine. Everyone's chill these days."
options.then: She looks doubtful. "You don't know that."

options.text: "Then maybe just keep it quiet forever."
options.then: She stares at her shoes. "Yeah. Maybe."

options.text: "If anyone's rude, I'll fight them."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Please don't. That'd make it worse."

steps.why: Steady support for whatever comes means more than promises you can't keep.

scenarios.relearn: Meet someone who shares with warmth and unchanged respect.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Rahul confided in you yesterday. Today he saw you laughing with your group, and he looks panicked.
scenarios.setup: He pulls you aside by the water cooler.

steps.prompt: Rahul asks: "Were you guys talking about me?"

options.text: "Relax. Not everything is about you."
options.then: Rahul flushes. "Right. Sorry I asked."

options.text: "No. What you told me stays with me."
options.then: His shoulders ease a little. "Sorry. I just got scared."

options.text: "No, but our friends would understand anyway."
options.then: He goes pale. "That's not your call to make."

options.text: "Why? Do you want me to tell them?"
options.then: He stares. "No. Why would you even ask that?"

steps.why: A clear, calm promise settles his fear.

steps.prompt: Rahul says: "I keep imagining everyone finding out."

options.text: "That sounds scary. It's yours to share, when you want."
options.then: He nods. "I just want to be the one who decides."

options.text: "Stop worrying so much. It'll all be fine."
options.then: He shrugs. "Easy for you to say."

options.text: "Maybe just tell everyone yourself. Then there's nothing to fear."
options.then: He looks alarmed. "I'm not ready for that."

options.text: "I'll keep an eye on who's gossiping and report back."
options.then: He hesitates. "That kind of makes it a bigger thing."

steps.why: Naming his fear, and that the story is his, helps him feel safe.

steps.prompt: Rahul asks: "What if someone asks you straight out?"

options.text: "I'll say it's not mine to talk about, and leave it."
options.then: Rahul nods. "Okay. That works. Thanks."

options.text: "I'll just tell them it's definitely not true."
options.then: Rahul winces. "Please don't say anything about me at all."

options.text: "I'll tell them to go and ask you."
options.then: His face falls. "Then they'll all come to me."

options.text: "Honestly, I'm a terrible liar. They'd probably know."
options.then: Rahul's panic comes back. "Then what do I do?"

steps.why: "Not mine to share" protects him without confirming or denying anything.

scenarios.relearn: Keep their confidence; their story is theirs alone to share.

scenarios.hook: Late at night, your friend Pooja calls, upset about questioning herself.
scenarios.setup: Her voice is small and shaky.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "I feel broken. Like no one else is like this."

options.text: "Yeah, that does sound like a lot is wrong."
options.then: Pooja goes quiet. "So it's not just me who thinks so."

options.text: "You're not broken, and you're not alone. I'm here."
options.then: She sniffs. "You really think so?"

options.text: "Don't cry. Crying won't fix anything."
options.then: She sniffs hard. "Sorry. I'll stop."

options.text: "Lots of people are like this, so it's no big deal."
options.then: She pauses. "It's a big deal to me."

steps.why: Hearing "not broken, not alone" answers the two fears she named.

steps.prompt: Pooja asks: "But what if I'm like this forever?"

options.text: "Then you'll be you forever. That's not a bad thing."
options.then: She laughs a little through tears. "Okay. I like that."

options.text: "Let's not think that far ahead."
options.then: She's quiet. "I can't help thinking about it."

options.text: "Don't say that. I promise everything will be perfect."
options.then: She sighs. "You can't know that."

options.text: "Honestly, I don't know what to tell you."
options.then: Pooja's voice drops. "Yeah. Nobody does."

steps.why: Being who you are is nothing to fear. Many people live happy, full lives.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "I've felt this low for weeks."

options.text: "Weeks? It'll pass. Just sleep on it."
options.then: "Okay," she says, her voice flat.

options.text: "That's a long time. Could we see the counsellor together?"
options.then: She hesitates. "Maybe. If you come with me."

options.text: "I'll keep this just between us two. I promise you."
options.then: "Thanks," she says quietly. You're left holding it alone, and worried.

options.text: "I'll tell your parents about it first thing tomorrow."
options.then: Pooja panics. "No! Please don't."

steps.why: Weeks of feeling low needs real support, and going together makes it easier.

steps.prompt: Pooja asks: "What if it gets bad tonight, after we hang up?"

options.text: "Just try to sleep. Things look better in the morning."
options.then: "Okay," she says, but she doesn't sound sure.

options.text: "Call Tele-MANAS 14416, or call me back. Either is fine."
options.then: She saves the number. "Okay. I'll call if I need to."

options.text: "I'll stay on the phone with you every night."
options.then: "Every night?" she asks. You both know that can't last.

options.text: "You'll be fine. You're stronger than you think."
options.then: "Maybe," she says, not sounding convinced.

steps.why: Tele-MANAS 14416 is there any hour, and your door stays open too.

scenarios.relearn: Tell a struggling friend they're not broken and not alone.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Sameer has spent an hour telling you about questioning himself.
scenarios.setup: Suddenly he reaches for his bag, looking embarrassed.

steps.prompt: Sameer says: "Sorry for dumping all this on you."

options.text: "You never have to apologise. I'm glad you told me."
options.then: He pauses, then sits back down. "Really?"

options.text: "It's fine. Just maybe keep it short next time."
options.then: He nods quickly. "Yeah. Sorry. Won't happen again."

options.text: "No worries. Anyway, did you see the match?"
options.then: He blinks. "Uh, yeah. The match." The moment closes.

options.text: "Bro, it's nothing. Everyone's got stuff."
options.then: He shrugs. "I guess mine's not that special."

steps.why: Telling him he never owes an apology welcomes him back, not away.

steps.prompt: Sameer asks: "Can I come to you again if it gets confusing?"

options.text: "Sure, as long as it's not too often."
options.then: He winces. "Right. I'll try not to."

options.text: "Yes. You can talk to me whenever you need."
options.then: He smiles a little. "Okay. That means a lot."

options.text: "You should talk to someone qualified, not me."
options.then: He goes quiet. "Right. Sorry."

options.text: "Only if you promise never to stress about it again."
options.then: He laughs awkwardly. "I can't promise that."

steps.why: Reassuring him plainly keeps the door open for next time.

steps.prompt: Sameer says: "I don't want to lean only on you, though."

options.text: "Then lean on no one. You've got this alone."
options.then: He forces a smile. "Right. Alone. Sure."

options.text: "Fair. The counsellor could be someone else to lean on."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Maybe. If you think it's okay."

options.text: "Tell the whole group, then. They'll help."
options.then: His eyes widen. "I'm not ready for that."

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll always be enough."
options.then: He smiles, unsure. "What if you're busy, though?"

steps.why: More than one support, like a counsellor, makes it lighter for both of you.

scenarios.relearn: Welcome a confiding friend warmly; they never owe an apology for trusting you.

scenarios.hook: In the library, your friend Anjali admits she's been questioning herself, and it's been really hard.
scenarios.setup: She's been staring at the same page for ages.

steps.prompt: Anjali says: "Nobody would get it. Not here, anyway."

options.text: "Maybe just wait and see if it sorts itself out."
options.then: She turns the page, then stops. "It hasn't so far, though."

options.text: "I'd like to try. And some people really do get it."
options.then: She looks up. "You really think so?"

options.text: "True. This place is pretty narrow-minded."
options.then: She sighs. "So I'm stuck, then."

options.text: "Come on. You're overreacting a bit."
options.then: Anjali shuts the book. "I'm not. I just don't know where to turn."

steps.why: Listening, and saying help exists, gives her hope without brushing it off.

steps.prompt: After a while, Anjali asks: "Who would I even talk to, though?"

options.text: "The school counsellor. Or Tele-MANAS 14416, any time."
options.then: She types the number into her phone. "Okay. That's something."

options.text: "Some online group. Strangers are easier to talk to."
options.then: She frowns. "Some of those groups are really mean."

options.text: "Your parents. They kind of have to help you."
options.then: She tenses. "You don't know my parents."

options.text: "Just me. You honestly don't need anyone else."
options.then: She smiles, but still looks worried. "You can't fix everything, though."

steps.why: A counsellor or Tele-MANAS 14416 offers real, caring support.

steps.prompt: Anjali asks: "What if a counsellor thinks something's wrong with me?"

options.text: "Then just don't tell them the real reason."
options.then: She frowns. "Then what's the point of going?"

options.text: "They might. People can be weird."
options.then: Anjali's face clouds. "Then why bother?"

options.text: "Nothing's wrong with you. Their job is to listen."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "Okay. Maybe I'll try."

options.text: "I'll call the counsellor for you and explain everything."
options.then: She tenses. "I'd rather tell it my own way."

steps.why: Nothing is wrong with her, and support is there to listen kindly.

scenarios.relearn: Gently point a struggling friend to a counsellor or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: "If you're not sure by now, something must be wrong with you."

myth.un: Being unsure about yourself means something is wrong with you.
myth.re: Being unsure is a normal part of understanding yourself; nothing is wrong with you.
myth.why: People come to understand themselves at very different paces.

scenarios.relearn: Being unsure isn't a flaw; understanding yourself takes the time it takes.

scenarios.hook: "You have to pick a label or you don't really count."

myth.un: You must pick a label to be valid or to 'really count'.
myth.re: You don't need any label to be valid; you're okay exactly as you are.
myth.why: Your worth never depended on naming or sorting yourself.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need a label to be valid; you're okay as you are.

scenarios.hook: "You owe people an explanation for how you feel."

myth.un: You owe others an explanation or proof of how you feel.
myth.re: You owe no one an explanation or proof; your feelings are yours.
myth.why: No one is entitled to your private feelings or a justification for them.

scenarios.relearn: You owe no one an explanation or proof of how you feel.

scenarios.hook: "Once you tell one person, you have to tell everyone."

myth.un: Telling one person means you must then tell everyone.
myth.re: Whether, when and who you tell is entirely your own choice, every time.
myth.why: Each decision to share is separate and always yours to make.

scenarios.relearn: Telling one person never obliges you to tell anyone else.

scenarios.hook: "Feeling this way means you'll never be happy."

myth.un: Questioning yourself means you'll never have a happy, full life.
myth.re: Many have walked this path to happy, full lives; there is real hope for yours too.
myth.why: Understanding yourself opens the door to a fuller life, not a smaller one.

scenarios.relearn: Questioning yourself doesn't doom your happiness; many live full, happy lives.

scenarios.hook: "Asking for help with this makes you weak."

myth.un: Reaching out for support with this makes you weak.
myth.re: Reaching for support takes courage; needing help sometimes is human, not weak.
myth.why: Everyone needs support at times; asking for it is a strength.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for support isn't weakness; it takes real courage.

scenarios.hook: "You're the only one who's ever felt this confused."

myth.un: You're the only one who has ever felt this unsure about yourself.
myth.re: You're far from alone; many people understand exactly this, and care.
myth.why: These questions are common and human, not unique to you.

scenarios.relearn: You're not the only one; many understand this and you're not alone.

scenarios.hook: In the canteen, a few boys start a slur-filled chant about Aman, a quieter classmate.

steps.prompt: Your own table starts joining in. What do you do?

options.text: Chant along so they don't turn on you
options.then: The chant gets louder, and Aman stares at his plate.

options.text: Say 'Leave it, yaar' and go sit with Aman
options.then: The chant falters, and Aman isn't alone at his table.

options.text: Leave the canteen so you're not part of it
options.then: You're out of it, but Aman is still there on his own.

options.text: Throw your water bottle at the loudest boy
options.then: Things explode, and a teacher marches you to the office.

steps.why: You don't need a scene. Not joining, and sitting with Aman, breaks the chant.

steps.prompt: Later, one of the boys says anyone who sits with Aman is 'on his team'. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're on the team of not being cruel
options.then: He laughs it off, but he doesn't push.

options.text: Laugh, and join the next joke about Aman
options.then: Aman hears, and looks down at his tiffin.

options.text: Threaten to beat him up
options.then: He squares up, and it nearly turns into a fight.

options.text: Shrug and say it's none of your business
options.then: He takes that as a yes, and the chant may start again tomorrow.

steps.why: A calm, simple line keeps you steady and shows where you stand.

steps.prompt: The next week, the chanting starts again and gets more aggressive. What do you do?

options.text: Film it for proof and post it
options.then: The video spreads, and Aman is humiliated again.

options.text: Gather friends to confront the boys
options.then: It turns into a shoving match.

options.text: Stay near Aman and tell a teacher straight away
options.then: A teacher steps in, and the boys back off.

options.text: Tell Aman to eat somewhere else for a while
options.then: Aman looks hurt. "So I'm the problem?"

steps.why: It's not Aman's fault. When it could turn unsafe, stay near him and get an adult.

scenarios.debrief: You needn't make a scene. Not joining, and quietly sitting with someone, counts.
scenarios.relearn: Don't join slurs; calmly decline and quietly support the person.

scenarios.hook: Groups are forming for the class trip to Jaipur, and Ritu keeps getting left out because of who she is.

options.text: Say 'Come with us' to Ritu and make room
options.then: Ritu smiles and adds her name to your list.

options.text: Ask your group to vote on whether she can join
options.then: Two hands go up slowly, and Ritu sees the hesitation.

options.text: Tell Ritu she can join if nobody else asks first
options.then: She nods, but she feels like a back-up plan.

steps.why: A simple 'come with us' is dignity in action.

steps.prompt: Later, a groupmate grumbles that Ritu makes trips 'awkward'. What do you say?

options.text: Agree, but say you felt bad for her
options.then: The groupmate nods, and Ritu becomes 'the pity case'.

options.text: Say she's just another classmate, and it'll be fine
options.then: The groupmate shrugs. "Okay, whatever."

options.text: Tell the groupmate to go find another group
options.then: Now there's a fight inside the group, days before the trip.

options.text: Promise to keep Ritu out of everyone's way
options.then: The groupmate is happy, and Ritu stays on the edges.

scenarios.hook: You're still working out your views when your hostel-mate Lalit gets shoved and slurred in the corridor.

steps.prompt: Two seniors are standing over him, laughing. What do you do?

options.text: Stay back, since you haven't made up your mind
options.then: The seniors carry on, and Lalit is alone with them.

options.text: Shout for the warden and go to Lalit's side
options.then: The seniors walk off fast, and Lalit gets up.

options.text: Square up to the seniors and tell them to try you
options.then: One shoves you too, and it starts to feel dangerous.

options.text: Go to your room and text the warden later
options.then: By the time the warden reads it, Lalit has faced it all alone.

steps.why: You don't need settled views to keep someone safe. Getting an adult protects you both.

steps.prompt: Lalit is sitting on the stairs, shaking. What do you say?

options.text: Say that wasn't okay, and ask if he's hurt
options.then: Lalit shakes his head. "Just my elbow." He wipes his eyes.

options.text: Ask what he did to make them so angry
options.then: Lalit's face hardens. "Nothing. I did nothing."

options.text: Tell him to keep to himself so it won't happen again
options.then: He nods slowly, looking smaller.

options.text: Say you don't really get his life, but whatever
options.then: He looks away. "Okay."

steps.why: Naming it as wrong, and checking on him, tells him it's not his fault.

steps.prompt: The next day, a friend asks why you'd even care, when you're 'not even sure' about all this. What do you say?

options.text: Say safety isn't about agreeing on everything
options.then: Your friend thinks. "Yeah, okay. Fair."

options.text: Say you only cared so the warden wouldn't blame you
options.then: Your friend nods, and the real point gets lost.

options.text: Say you shouldn't have, and won't next time
options.then: Your friend nods, and you feel uneasy all day.

options.text: Tell your friend they're heartless for asking
options.then: Your friend bristles, and the talk turns into a fight.

steps.why: Dignity and safety are for everyone, whatever your views.

steps.prompt: A week later, the seniors start following Lalit around the hostel. What do you do?

options.text: Tell Lalit to stay in his room until it blows over
options.then: Lalit stays in, missing meals and his friends.

options.text: Go with Lalit to report it to the warden
options.then: The warden calls the seniors in, and Lalit sleeps easier.

options.text: Follow the seniors to see what they're up to
options.then: They notice you and turn on you instead.

options.text: Post about them anonymously in the hostel group
options.then: The post sparks gossip, and the seniors get angrier at Lalit.

steps.why: Ongoing targeting needs an adult, and going together means he isn't alone.

scenarios.debrief: You can keep someone safe while still working out your own views.
scenarios.relearn: Safety is never conditional on agreeing; the dignity floor is for all.

options.text: Hint at it without saying it outright
options.then: Sana's eyes widen. She has her answer.

options.text: Say 'I can't say, but you're not wrong'

options.text: Tell her to go ahead, since it's his business anyway
options.then: Sana corners Karan by the lockers, and he looks shaken.

options.text: Offer to ask him for her, more gently

options.then: Sana storms off, and the rumour sticks around.

options.text: React with a shocked emoji
options.then: The rumour gets more replies.

options.text: Reply 'Not ours to talk about' and move the chat on

options.text: Leave the chat without saying anything
options.then: The rumour carries on without you.

options.text: Sit with him and chat about normal things

options.text: Leave him alone, so you don't make it worse

steps.why: Ordinary company, with no prying, tells him he isn't alone.

scenarios.debrief: Whether, when and to whom anyone shares anything is only ever their choice.

options.text: Send it to a friend to ask if they've seen it

options.text: Wait for her to bring it up first

options.text: Ask her if what the reel says is true

scenarios.hook: Your friends are filming a 'roast' video about a group of students for who they are, and want you in it.

scenarios.debrief: For situations that could turn unsafe, support the person and get an adult.

scenarios.hook: At a family dinner, your uncle makes a cutting remark about 'those people' in the news.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "What? I'm only saying what everyone thinks."

options.text: "That's bigoted, uncle. You should be ashamed."
options.then: The table goes silent. "Is this what they teach you now?" he snaps.

options.text: "Can we please not talk about this at dinner?"
options.then: "Fine, fine," he says. "Pass the dal."

options.text: "Let's not, uncle. Everyone deserves respect."

steps.why: A gentle line about respect holds the floor without attacking him in front of everyone.

options.text: "You don't have to agree. Respect is still for everyone."

options.text: "Yes. And honestly, you're behind the times."
options.then: "Behind the times? Watch your tone," he says.

options.text: "No, no. Not really, uncle. Forget it."
options.then: "Good," he says. "I thought so."

options.text: "Let's just change the topic, please, uncle."
options.then: "Fine. You young people are too sensitive," he says.

steps.why: Separating belief from basic respect means he can keep his views without the put-downs.

steps.prompt: After dinner, your mother asks: "Should we say something when he talks like that, or let it go?"

options.text: "Let it go. He's never going to change."
options.then: "Maybe," she sighs. "It just sits badly with me."

options.text: "Next time, I'll argue it out with him properly."
options.then: "Please," she says. "Not a big fight at the table."

options.text: "A calm word, yes. Respect isn't something to skip."
options.then: She nods. "Next time, I'll back you up."

options.text: "Only if someone it's about is at the table."
options.then: "So it's fine when they're not there?" she asks.
