scenarios.hook: Near the school gate, two seniors have cornered your classmate Rhea and are mocking her.
scenarios.setup: You see it from across the road and walk over.

steps.prompt: One senior turns and says: "What do you want? We're just talking to her."

options.text: "What's wrong with you lot? Leave her alone!"
options.then: The senior steps closer. "Or what?"

options.text: "Hey Rhea, I was looking for you. Let's go."
options.then: Rhea grabs her bag. "Yeah, coming." The seniors let her go.

options.text: "Oh. Sorry. Never mind, then."
options.then: The senior smirks. "Thought so." Rhea is still stuck there.

options.text: "Guys, come on. It's really not worth it."
options.then: "Mind your business," he says, and turns back to Rhea.

steps.why: A casual line gets her out fast without turning it into a face-off.

steps.prompt: Later, Rhea finds you in the library and says: "They do this every week. Please don't tell anyone."

options.text: "Okay. It stays between us. I promise."
options.then: "Thanks," she says. Next week, they're at the gate again.

options.text: "Every week? You should've reported it ages ago."
options.then: Rhea's face closes. "I knew you'd say that."

options.text: "I hear you. But a teacher can stop this. I'll come too."
options.then: Rhea hesitates. "If you stay with me, maybe."

options.text: "Then let's walk out together every day from now on."
options.then: "That helps," she says. "But you're not here on Saturdays."

steps.why: It's not her fault. Staying with her and reaching a teacher is what stops it.

steps.prompt: Rhea asks quietly: "If I do tell a teacher, what if they think I'm making a fuss?"

options.text: "They might. Maybe wait and see if it stops."
options.then: "Yeah. Maybe it'll stop," she says, not sounding sure.

options.text: "Then we'll handle the seniors ourselves."
options.then: "I don't want you getting hurt too," she says.

options.text: "Then we try the counsellor. You deserve to feel safe."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Let's go before I lose my nerve."

options.text: "I'll tell the teacher for you. You don't need to come."
options.then: "But I want to say it myself," she says quietly.

steps.why: If one adult doesn't listen, another will. Her safety is worth asking again.

scenarios.relearn: A casual 'let's go' defuses and removes someone from harm without escalation.

scenarios.hook: In the canteen, your friend Simran leans in, about to tell the table something private about a classmate.
scenarios.setup: You catch her eye before she starts.

steps.prompt: Simran whispers to you: "Wait till they hear this about Arnav. It's huge."

options.text: "Go on. Everyone's curious anyway."
options.then: Simran grins. "Okay. Let me get everyone's attention."

options.text: "Careful. That's not ours to tell."
options.then: Simran pauses. "Hm. Okay, maybe not here."

options.text: "Tell me first. Just me."
options.then: Simran whispers it to you. Now two people know.

options.text: "You're such a gossip. Seriously."
options.then: "Wow. Rude," she says. "I'm telling them anyway."

steps.why: Stopping it quietly, before it's said, protects him without embarrassing her.

steps.prompt: Simran adds: "And it's true, by the way. I'm not making anything up."

options.text: "True or not, it's only gossip. Who cares?"
options.then: "Exactly. So it's fine to tell," she says, turning to the table.

options.text: "Then just tell a couple of people, not everyone."
options.then: "Okay. Only Meera and Dev, then," she says.

options.text: "Even if it's true, it's his to share. Not ours."
options.then: "Fair," she says. "I'd hate it if someone did that to me."

options.text: "Prove it, then. Show me the messages."
options.then: "Hang on. I'll find them," she says, scrolling.

steps.why: Something being true doesn't make it ours to tell. Privacy can be about safety.

steps.prompt: Later, Simran asks: "Should I tell Arnav I know? Or pretend I don't?"

options.text: "Ask him straight out. Clear the air."
options.then: "Maybe," she says. "I'll catch him after class."

options.text: "Drop hints, so he knows you're okay with it."
options.then: "Like jokes?" she asks. "He might hate that."

options.text: "Tell him who told you, so he knows who to avoid."
options.then: "That'll start a whole fight," she says.

options.text: "Let him lead. Just treat him the same as always."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "Same old Arnav, then."

steps.why: He decides whether and when to share. Treating him the same is respect.

myth.re: Everyone's safety and dignity isn't a debate position; it's the floor we all stand on.
myth.why: Safety being non-negotiable is settled ground, not a contest of opinions.

scenarios.relearn: Keeping someone safe isn't taking a side; safety is the floor, not a debate.

scenarios.hook: "If nobody talked about it, it would just disappear."

myth.un: Silence would make this diversity go away.
myth.re: Silence doesn't change who people are; it only leaves them more alone and unsafe.
myth.why: People exist whether or not anyone names it; silence just adds harm.

scenarios.relearn: Silence doesn't erase who people are; it only isolates them.

scenarios.hook: "You can pray or train it away if you try hard enough."

myth.un: Enough effort or prayer can change who someone is.
myth.re: Effort can't change who a person is; 'change' attempts are discredited and often cause real harm.
myth.why: Trying to change someone hurts them; it doesn't work.

scenarios.relearn: No amount of effort changes who someone is; 'change' attempts only harm.

scenarios.hook: "It must have been something the parents did wrong."

myth.un: A child is gay or trans because their parents made a mistake.
myth.re: It isn't caused by parenting or any 'mistake'; it's simply part of who the person is.
myth.why: Blaming parents adds guilt to a thing nobody did or could prevent.

scenarios.relearn: It isn't anyone's 'fault' or a parenting error; it's just who someone is.

scenarios.hook: "Calling it normal just encourages more of it."

myth.un: Saying this is normal makes more people 'become' it.
myth.re: Naming something as natural doesn't increase it; it just lets people who already vary feel safe.
myth.why: Acceptance changes how safe people feel, not who they are.

scenarios.relearn: Calling it normal doesn't 'encourage' it; it only helps people feel safe.

scenarios.hook: "They can hide it, so there's no real harm in mocking."

myth.un: Mockery is harmless because the person can just hide who they are.
myth.re: Forcing someone to hide and mocking them both cause real harm; neither is harmless.
myth.why: Asking a person to disappear to avoid your jokes isn't a kindness.

scenarios.relearn: Mockery isn't harmless; making someone hide who they are causes real harm.

scenarios.hook: "Real men and women don't question any of this."

myth.un: Anyone who questions their gender or whom they love is weak or confused.
myth.re: Working out who you are takes honesty and courage; it isn't weakness or confusion.
myth.why: Questioning is a normal, brave part of growing up for many people.

scenarios.relearn: Questioning who you are isn't weakness; it's an honest, normal part of life.

scenarios.hook: "It's a sickness you can pass to younger siblings."

myth.un: A younger sibling can 'catch' it from an older one.
myth.re: It isn't a sickness and isn't catchable; siblings don't pass who they are to each other.
myth.why: You can't transmit who a person is like a cold.

scenarios.relearn: It's neither a sickness nor catchable; nobody passes it to a sibling.

scenarios.hook: "Standing up for them puts your own family's honour at risk."

myth.un: Showing a classmate basic respect dishonours your family.
myth.re: Treating someone with dignity reflects well on you; cruelty is what brings shame.
myth.why: Kindness and fairness are values most families are proud of.

scenarios.relearn: Basic respect for someone never dishonours your family; cruelty does.

scenarios.hook: "They chose this life, so any problems are their own fault."

myth.un: They 'chose' it, so they deserve whatever hardship follows.
myth.re: It isn't a choice, and even if it were, nobody deserves cruelty or unsafety.
myth.why: Dignity and safety aren't a reward for choosing 'correctly'.

scenarios.relearn: It isn't a choice, and no one deserves cruelty for who they are.

scenarios.hook: "Accepting people like this means abandoning all our values."

myth.un: Respecting LGBTQ people means giving up your own values.
myth.re: You can keep your own beliefs and still hold the shared value that everyone deserves dignity.
myth.why: Treating people kindly sits alongside your values, it doesn't replace them.

scenarios.relearn: Respect for everyone sits alongside your values; it doesn't erase them.

scenarios.hook: "If it were normal, why do they stay so quiet about it?"

myth.un: Staying quiet proves there's something wrong with it.
myth.re: People often stay quiet because of fear of mockery or harm, not because anything is wrong.
myth.why: Silence is usually about safety, not shame.

scenarios.relearn: People stay quiet for safety, not because anything is wrong with them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a myth can be wrong AND the person who repeated it can still deserve patience. Both?
scenarios.affirm: Holding the idea to a high standard while holding the person gently is exactly the balance this game builds.
scenarios.relearn: You can reject a false idea and still be patient with the person who held it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: notice the gap between 'I disagree with you' and 'you should be unsafe'. Real difference?
scenarios.affirm: Disagreement is fair game; someone's safety never is. Keeping those apart is the whole skill.
scenarios.relearn: Disagreeing with someone and wanting them unsafe are not the same thing.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which lands better when you correct a myth, 'you're an idiot' or 'actually, here's the truth'?
scenarios.affirm: Calm facts change more minds than insults ever do, and they keep the door open.
scenarios.relearn: Calm facts persuade better than insults and keep the conversation open.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: misinformation, not the people, is the real danger here. Sit with that for a second?
scenarios.affirm: When fear is replaced with facts, fewer people get hurt. That's why getting it right matters.
scenarios.relearn: Accurate understanding reduces harm; misinformation is the real danger.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you don't have to win an argument to keep someone safe. Does that take pressure off?
scenarios.affirm: Standing quietly by someone's dignity counts, even when you never 'win' the debate.
scenarios.relearn: You can protect someone's dignity without needing to win any argument.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I don't fully get it, but I'll still be kind' is an honest, good place to stand. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: You can be unsure and respectful at the same time; understanding can grow while kindness stays.
scenarios.relearn: You can still be unsure about something and choose to be respectful and kind.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when a 'fact' about a whole group sounds like an insult, that's a clue. Worth a pause?
scenarios.affirm: Claims that exist mainly to put a group down are usually myths, not facts. Pausing to check is wise.
scenarios.relearn: A 'fact' that mainly insults a whole group is usually a myth worth questioning.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: respect doesn't mean knowing everything private about someone. Relieving?
scenarios.affirm: You can respect someone fully without learning a single private thing about them.
scenarios.relearn: You can respect people without knowing anything private about them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: it's okay to update what you once believed about all this. Does growing your view feel okay?
scenarios.affirm: Changing your mind when you learn more isn't a weakness; it's exactly how understanding grows.
scenarios.relearn: Updating an old belief when you learn more is a strength, not a weakness.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'people simply vary, and always have' is the quiet truth under most of these myths. Sit with it?
scenarios.affirm: Once 'people vary, and always have' is your starting point, most of the myths quietly fall away.
scenarios.relearn: People simply vary, and always have; that one truth undoes most of the myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: which line corrects kindly, and which one wounds the person?

items.text: "That's a common myth; here's what's true."
"I used to think that too, then learned more."

scenarios.relearn: Sharing the truth or your own learning corrects kindly; name-calling wounds and changes no minds.

scenarios.hook: Sort: an honest difference of belief, or the dignity floor that isn't up for debate?

items.text: What a wedding looks like in my family
Whether a classmate deserves to be safe
Whether anyone may be bullied for who they are
How I'd raise my own children
Whether every person is owed respect

scenarios.relearn: Beliefs about weddings or raising kids can differ; everyone's safety and respect can't.

scenarios.hook: Sort: which of these can you actually 'catch' from being near it, and which you can't?

items.text: The flu from a sick friend
Who a person is, from sitting beside them

scenarios.relearn: Germs spread; who a person is doesn't. You can't 'catch' someone's orientation or identity.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a thing people genuinely choose, or a thing that's just part of who they are?

items.text: Your own inner sense of your gender
Whom you fall in love with

scenarios.relearn: You choose hobbies and studies; you don't choose who you're drawn to or your sense of self.

scenarios.hook: Sort: India's own past, or a recent 'import'?

items.text: Diversity acknowledged in India's old traditions
"It only arrived from the West recently"
Varied identities across India's long history
People who varied, here, for centuries

scenarios.relearn: This diversity runs through India's own long history; the 'foreign import' line is the myth.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a settled fact about health and identity, or a discredited 'illness' claim?

items.text: It was removed from illness classifications long ago
"It needs a doctor to cure it"
Health bodies say it isn't an illness

scenarios.relearn: Health bodies long ago said it isn't an illness; 'cure', 'disorder' and 'fix' are discredited.

scenarios.hook: Sort: which words name someone with respect, and which are slurs or put-downs?

items.text: The word a person uses for themselves
Asking kindly which term they prefer
"My friend" with no label at all
A mocking nickname about who they are

scenarios.relearn: Use the words people use for themselves, or just 'my friend'; slurs and mocking labels never respect.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a response that keeps the dignity floor, or one that quietly chips at it?

items.text: Sitting with the person left out

scenarios.relearn: Declining slurs and including people keeps the dignity floor; 'only a joke' and laughing along chip at it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: corrects a myth with a real reason, or just asserts with nothing behind it?

items.text: "Health bodies say it isn't an illness."
"It's in India's history, so not foreign."
"Nobody chooses it, so it isn't a choice."

scenarios.relearn: A myth is best met with a real reason, not 'it just is' or 'everyone knows'.

scenarios.hook: Sort: true things to say, or harmful myths to never repeat?

items.text: "You're not broken; this is just who you are."
"You could change if you really tried."
"People have always varied; you're not alone."
"It's a phase; you'll grow out of it."

scenarios.relearn: 'You're not broken' and 'people vary' are true; 'change', 'phase' and 'caught it' are myths.

scenarios.hook: At a family dinner, talk turns to a celebrity's interview, and your uncle scoffs.
scenarios.setup: He turns to you, the only teenager at the table.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "It's just a phase. All teens go through it."

options.text: "Ugh, uncle, that's such an old-fashioned thing to say."
options.then: "Old-fashioned? Have some respect," he says.

options.text: "For many people it lasts, uncle. It's not ours to time."
options.then: Uncle pauses. "Hm. You think so?"

options.text: "Maybe. Who really knows, uncle?"
options.then: He nods. "Exactly. They'll grow out of it."

options.text: "Can we not talk about this right now, please?"
options.then: "Fine, fine. Touchy topic," he chuckles.

steps.why: Stating the truth calmly corrects the myth without attacking him.

steps.prompt: Your uncle asks: "And why do we hear about it so much more these days?"

options.text: "Because of the internet, obviously. It's basically a trend."
options.then: "Exactly. A trend," he says, satisfied.

options.text: "Because people like you made them hide before."
options.then: His face hardens. "So now I'm the villain?"

options.text: "People feel safer saying it now. It was always there."
options.then: He thinks. "Hm. My own nani did say life was never simple."

options.text: "I don't know, uncle. Pass the rice?"
options.then: He laughs and moves on, the idea unchallenged.

steps.why: More people speak up because it's safer now, not because more people are this way.

steps.prompt: Your uncle asks: "So what are we older people supposed to say about it?"

options.text: "Honestly, just keep your opinions to yourself."
options.then: "In my own house? Interesting," he says.

options.text: "You need to read up and change your views."
options.then: "I'm too old for homework, beta."

options.text: "Nothing special. Just treat people with respect."
options.then: "That much I can do," he says, and smiles.

options.text: "Whatever you like. It's your opinion, uncle."
options.then: "Good. Then it's a phase," he says.

steps.why: Respect is the floor, and it's simple. He doesn't need perfect words to keep it.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly stating the truth corrects the myth without attacking the person.

scenarios.hook: After a health class, your classmate Varun hangs back to ask you something.
scenarios.setup: He keeps his voice low.

steps.prompt: Varun asks: "You can't catch being gay, right? Someone said you can."

options.text: "Honestly, I'm not sure. Maybe you can?"
options.then: Varun frowns. "So I should be careful?"

options.text: "Who told you that? Tell me and I'll sort them out."
options.then: Varun looks alarmed. "No, it's fine. I just wanted to know."

options.text: "Ask Sir. I don't really want to get into it."
options.then: Varun hesitates. "Sir's busy. I'd rather just ask you."

options.text: "Right. You can't catch it. People are who they are."
options.then: Varun exhales. "Okay. That's what I thought."

steps.why: A simple, true answer clears up the myth before it turns into fear.

steps.prompt: Varun asks: "So why do some parents tell their kids to stay away?"

options.text: "Because those parents are just stupid."
options.then: Varun stiffens. "Hey. My mum said that."

options.text: "Some people have heard myths. Fear isn't fact."
options.then: "Yeah," he says. "Maybe I'll tell my mum that."

options.text: "Maybe they know something we don't."
options.then: "So it can spread?" Varun asks.

options.text: "No idea. Parents worry about everything, honestly."
options.then: "True," he laughs, still half unsure.

steps.why: Naming myths as myths, without insulting anyone's family, keeps the facts clear.

steps.prompt: Varun asks: "Some of my friends say it too. What would you tell them?"

options.text: "Nothing. They won't listen anyway."
options.then: "Yeah, probably not," he says, and drops it.

options.text: "That they're idiots for believing it."
options.then: "That'll go well," Varun says, rolling his eyes.

options.text: "Just this, simply: you can't catch who someone is."
options.then: "That's short. I could say that," he says.

options.text: "I'd send them a long video that explains it all."
options.then: "They'll never watch it," he says.

steps.why: A short, kind fact is easy to share, and it doesn't put anyone down.

scenarios.relearn: Identity isn't contagious; you can't 'catch' who someone is.

scenarios.hook: In the school library, your friend Gaurav scrolls past a post and mutters something.
scenarios.setup: He turns his phone to show you.

steps.prompt: Gaurav says: "This is all a Western thing. It's not Indian."

options.text: "You clearly don't know any history at all."
options.then: "Wow, okay, professor," he snaps.

options.text: "Maybe. I guess it could be foreign."
options.then: "See? Even you agree," he says. "Unless there's some history I've missed."

options.text: "Actually, it runs through India's own history too."
options.then: Gaurav squints. "Really? Like where?"

options.text: "It doesn't matter where it's from, honestly."
options.then: "Doesn't matter? It's about our culture," he says.

steps.why: The history is real, and sharing it calmly corrects the myth.

steps.prompt: Gaurav asks: "So is there anything like it in our own history?"

options.text: "Look it up yourself. I'm not your history teacher."
options.then: "Then I'll assume you made it up," he grins.

options.text: "Yes. Our own traditions have long acknowledged it."
options.then: Gaurav pauses. "Huh. I didn't know it went back that far."

options.text: "I can't remember the details right now, but trust me."
options.then: "Trust you? Come on," he laughs.

options.text: "Obviously. Everyone knows that except you."
options.then: "That's a bit rude," he mutters.

steps.why: India's own long traditions show it isn't imported. Saying so calmly turns an argument into a fact.

steps.prompt: Gaurav says: "Still. My family would never accept it."

options.text: "Then your family is the problem."
options.then: "Leave my family out of it," he says.

options.text: "They don't have to agree. Respect is still for all."
options.then: Gaurav nods slowly. "Respect, yeah. That I get."

options.text: "Fair. Some things just aren't for people like us."
options.then: "Exactly," he says, and the myth settles back in.

options.text: "Then just don't bring it up at home."
options.then: "Easy," he says. "Nobody does anyway."

steps.why: Beliefs can differ. Respect is the floor, and it asks no one to give up their family.

scenarios.relearn: This diversity spans cultures and India's own history; it isn't a foreign import.

scenarios.hook: Your aunt shows you an ad for a clinic that claims it can 'cure' people of who they love.
scenarios.setup: She seems worried, not unkind.

steps.prompt: Your aunt asks: "Is it an illness, then? This says it can be treated."

options.text: "Maybe. They must know what they're doing."
options.then: "Hm. I'll forward it to the family group, then," she says.

options.text: "No. It isn't an illness, so there's nothing to cure."
options.then: She frowns at the ad. "Then what are they selling?"

options.text: "That's a scam, Masi. Why are you even reading it?"
options.then: She looks hurt. "I was only asking, beta."

options.text: "I don't know. It's not really my area, Masi."
options.then: "Well, it looks very official," she says, unsure.

steps.why: It isn't an illness. Saying so plainly protects people from false 'cures'.

steps.prompt: Your aunt asks: "Is there any harm in trying, if a family wants it?"

options.text: "No harm, I guess, if they really want to."
options.then: "Right. It's their choice," she says.

options.text: "Only if the person agrees to it, I suppose."
options.then: "So if they agree, it's fine?" she asks.

options.text: "Honestly, families who do that are terrible."
options.then: She stiffens. "Families worry. That's not terrible."

options.text: "These 'cures' don't work, and they cause real harm."
options.then: She sets the phone down. "I didn't know that."

steps.why: So-called cures hurt people. Being clear about that can prevent real harm.

steps.prompt: Your aunt asks: "If a family is worried, where should they go, then?"

options.text: "To a doctor who can fix it properly."
options.then: "So it is something to fix?" she asks.

options.text: "A counsellor. Not a clinic that claims to cure."
options.then: She nods. "A counsellor. That sounds more sensible."

options.text: "Nowhere. They should just get over it."
options.then: "That's easy to say," she sighs.

options.text: "Just search online. There's loads of information."
options.then: "Online is where I found this ad," she says.

steps.why: A supportive counsellor helps families with worries, without treating anyone as ill.

scenarios.relearn: It is not an illness. There is nothing to 'cure', and 'change' attempts cause harm.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Mohit says he's done being polite to people whose lives he doesn't agree with.
scenarios.setup: You're walking to the bus together.

steps.prompt: Mohit asks: "I disagree with all this. So why should I be nice to them?"

options.text: "You have to agree with me, or you're just wrong."
options.then: "Then I'm wrong. Happy?" he snaps.

options.text: "Fine. Don't bother being nice, then."
options.then: "Good. I won't," he shrugs.

options.text: "Keep your views. But basic respect is for everyone."
options.then: Mohit kicks a stone. "Even if I don't agree?"

options.text: "Just avoid them, then. Easier for everyone."
options.then: "Fine. I'll pretend they don't exist."

steps.why: You can hold your beliefs and still owe everyone dignity and safety.

steps.prompt: Mohit says: "Being polite feels fake if I don't agree."

options.text: "Then be fake. Who cares, honestly?"
options.then: "So it's all just an act," he says.

options.text: "Then maybe your views are the actual problem here."
options.then: "So you're judging me now?" he asks.

options.text: "Just be polite when teachers are around."
options.then: "Got it. Polite when it counts," he grins.

options.text: "It's not agreeing. It's how you'd want to be treated."
options.then: Mohit is quiet. "Yeah. I'd hate being treated like that."

steps.why: Respect isn't a stamp of agreement. It's the basic floor everyone deserves.

steps.prompt: Mohit asks: "And if my friends mock them? Do I have to step in?"

options.text: "At least don't join in. Say it's not okay, if you can."
options.then: "Not joining in, I can do," he says. "The rest, I'll try."

options.text: "Not your problem. Just stay out of it."
options.then: "Cool. Easier that way," he says.

options.text: "Yes. You have to fight them every single time."
options.then: "Fight my own friends? No way."

options.text: "Only if it gets physical. Words are just words, right?"
options.then: "So words are fine till then?" he asks.

steps.why: Safety isn't up for debate. Not joining in, and saying so, protects people.

scenarios.relearn: You can hold your own beliefs and still owe everyone dignity and safety.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Kiran posted proudly about who he is, and your friend Tanya scoffs at it.
scenarios.setup: She holds out her phone to you.

steps.prompt: Tanya says: "He just wants attention. Obviously."

options.text: "You're so shallow for saying that."
options.then: "Wow. Okay," Tanya says, hurt.

options.text: "Haha, totally. Classic Kiran."
options.then: Tanya grins and starts typing a comment.

options.text: "Most people risk a lot to share that. It's not attention."
options.then: Tanya pauses. "Risk? I didn't think of it like that."

options.text: "Maybe. But it's his account, so whatever, honestly."
options.then: "Whatever is right," she says, still smirking.

steps.why: Sharing who you are usually takes courage, not a need for attention.

steps.prompt: Tanya asks: "Why would anyone even post something like that?"

options.text: "To get likes. Same as everyone else does."
options.then: "See? Attention," she says.

options.text: "Maybe so he doesn't have to hide. His call."
options.then: Tanya pauses. "I guess hiding would be tiring."

options.text: "Why do you care so much about what he posts?"
options.then: "I don't," she says, defensive.

options.text: "No idea. You should ask Kiran directly."
options.then: "Ha, maybe I will," she says.

steps.why: Whether and how someone shares is entirely their own choice.

steps.prompt: Tanya says: "Some people in our class are already making fun of the post."

options.text: "His post, his problem, I guess."
options.then: "True," she shrugs, and scrolls on.

options.text: "Let's call them all out in the comments."
options.then: "That'll just start a war," she says.

options.text: "Kiran should delete it, to avoid trouble."
options.then: "Yeah, probably safer," she says.

options.text: "Let's report the worst comments, and leave a kind one."
options.then: Tanya hesitates. "Okay. Reporting, and a heart."

steps.why: Reporting abuse instead of piling on, plus a little kindness, supports Kiran's dignity.

steps.prompt: Next day, Tanya says: "Kiran looks really low today. Should we say anything?"

options.text: "Better not. We'll only make it awkward for him."
options.then: "Yeah, true," she says. Kiran eats lunch alone.

options.text: "Let's tell him who's been making fun of his post."
options.then: "Won't that make him feel worse?" she asks.

options.text: "Sit with him. Offer to see a teacher together."
options.then: "Okay," Tanya says. "Lunch first. Then a teacher, if he wants."

options.text: "Let's send him a long message about how brave he is."
options.then: "Isn't that a bit much?" she asks. "He'd hate a fuss."

steps.why: Friendliness tells him he belongs. A teacher can stop the mocking, which is never his fault.

scenarios.relearn: It isn't done for attention; it's a real part of who someone is.

scenarios.hook: After a club meeting, a quiet junior, Meera, waits until the others have left.
scenarios.setup: She speaks without looking up.

steps.prompt: Meera asks: "Is there something wrong with people who love differently?"

options.text: "That's not really my place to say, sorry."
options.then: She nods quickly. "Okay. Sorry I asked."

options.text: "No. Nothing's wrong. People simply vary, and always have."
options.then: Meera looks up. "Really? Nobody ever says that."

options.text: "Don't ask things like that around here."
options.then: Meera goes pale and half-stands, then slowly sits back down.

options.text: "Of course not! Don't you worry about that at all, okay?"
options.then: She nods, but she still looks unsure.

steps.why: A plain, true answer that nothing is wrong is what she most needs to hear.

steps.prompt: Meera hesitates, then says: "Some people at home say it's a sickness."

options.text: "Your family must be really backward, then."
options.then: "Don't say that about them," she says quietly.

options.text: "Ignore them. They'll come around one day."
options.then: "They don't seem like they will," she says.

options.text: "It isn't. Health experts agree it's not an illness."
options.then: Meera breathes out. "I kept wondering if they were right."

options.text: "Maybe they know best. They're your family, after all."
options.then: She looks down. "Yeah. Maybe."

steps.why: Correcting the myth gently, without putting her family down, keeps her safe and heard.

steps.prompt: Meera says: "I just feel really alone sometimes."

options.text: "Everyone feels alone at our age. It's totally normal."
options.then: "Yeah. I guess," she says, and goes quiet.

options.text: "You should tell your family how you feel."
options.then: She tenses. "I can't. Not yet."

options.text: "You're not alone. Our counsellor is kind, if you want."
options.then: "Maybe," she says. "Would you show me where her room is?"

options.text: "Pick a label. It'll make things way easier."
options.then: "I don't even know what I'd pick," she says.

steps.why: Reassurance plus a safe adult she can choose means she has real support.

scenarios.relearn: There's nothing wrong with anyone for who they are; people simply vary, and always have.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin Dev changes the channel when a show talks about people who love differently.
scenarios.setup: Your little cousins are watching too.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "If we just don't talk about it, it'll go away."

options.text: "That's a ridiculous thing to believe, Dev."
options.then: "Ridiculous? Okay, genius," he says.

options.text: "Sure. Let's just never talk about it."
options.then: "Exactly. Problem solved," he says.

options.text: "Silence doesn't change who people are. It isolates them."
options.then: Dev frowns. "Isolates them? I never thought of that."

options.text: "Fine. Just don't change the channel on me again."
options.then: "Fine," he says, switching back. The idea stays.

steps.why: Silence doesn't erase who anyone is. It only isolates them.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "Talking about it just confuses kids."

options.text: "You're right. Let's keep the little ones out of it."
options.then: "Good. Simple," he says.

options.text: Say you don't know, so maybe wait a bit

steps.prompt: When Aryan does see the counsellor, with you there, she asks to see the messages. He hesitates. What do you do?

options.text: Sit beside him and let him choose what to show

steps.prompt: That evening, Aryan asks what he should do if more messages come. What do you say?

options.text: Say they'll stop, now that an adult knows

options.text: Say you'll deal with them yourself next time

options.text: Say he'll just have to be braver next time

steps.why: Knowing where to turn, any time, means he never has to face it alone.

scenarios.debrief: When bullying could turn unsafe, it's never the person's fault: support them and get a trusted adult.
scenarios.relearn: If threats turn scary, gently help them reach a counsellor or adult.

options.text: Say nothing. She'll want to be left alone

options.text: Tell her everyone has seen it by now anyway

steps.prompt: After class, Lavanya says quietly that she doesn't know what to do now. What do you suggest?

scenarios.debrief: Don't spread screenshots that out or mock someone. Report it and support them.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Tenzin is bullied on the school bus, and you worry helping will make you the next target.

options.text: Stand up and give the bullies a speech

options.text: Assume it'll stop on its own soon enough

options.text: Tip off a teacher you trust, privately

options.text: Tell Tenzin to sit right at the front next time

options.text: Get your friends to tease the bullies back
options.then: The bus turns into a shouting match.

steps.why: An adult can change things on the bus. Telling quietly keeps you safe too.

steps.prompt: A bully notices you looking over and asks if you're Tenzin's friend now. What do you do?

options.text: Believe it's your own fault for getting involved
options.then: You start dreading the bus yourself.

options.text: Keep it to yourself so you don't seem weak

options.then: Tenzin notices, and sits alone again.

options.then: The bully loses interest, and the teacher keeps an eye out.

steps.prompt: A week later, Tenzin asks you whether people think he deserves it. What do you say?

options.text: Say some people probably do, honestly
options.then: His face falls. "I knew it."

options.text: Say no one deserves it, and you like his company

options.text: Say not to worry about what people think

steps.why: Saying no one deserves bullying, and that you value him, tells him it isn't his fault.

scenarios.debrief: Safe upstanding, quiet support plus an adult, never requires making yourself a target.
scenarios.relearn: Help safely: sit with them and tip off a teacher; no showdown needed.

scenarios.hook: You told your class teacher about bullying of a classmate, Gauri, over who she is. She called it 'kids being kids'.

options.text: Give up. Clearly no adult is going to help
options.then: The bullying goes on, and Gauri stops coming to lunch.

options.text: Calmly tell the counsellor what you've seen
options.then: The counsellor listens and asks to meet Gauri.

options.text: Confront the bullies yourself, since no one else will
options.then: They laugh, and turn on Gauri harder.

options.text: Wait a week, then tell the same teacher again
options.then: She brushes it off a second time.

steps.why: One adult brushing it off isn't the end. Another trusted adult can still help.

steps.prompt: Soon, the school counsellor asks to see you. She is looking into how Gauri is treated and wants the details. What do you do?

options.text: Repeat what others say about Gauri's private life
options.then: The counsellor stops you gently. "Let's stick to what you saw."

options.text: Exaggerate a little so she takes it seriously
options.then: She asks a detail you can't answer, and looks unsure.

options.text: Say what you saw, plainly, with no guessing
options.then: The counsellor nods. "That's very clear. Thank you."

options.text: Say you'd rather not get involved
options.then: She nods. Without details, she can't do much.

steps.why: Plain facts help an adult act, and Gauri's privacy stays hers.

steps.prompt: Gauri finds out you told, and asks you why. What do you say?

options.text: Say it wasn't you who told

options.text: Say she should have told someone herself
options.then: Gauri shrinks back.

options.text: Say you wanted her safe, and none of it is her fault
options.then: Gauri's eyes fill. "I thought nobody cared."

options.text: Say sorry, and promise never to tell anyone anything again
options.then: "Okay," she says, still unsure who she can trust.

steps.why: Being honest, and saying it isn't her fault, helps her trust that help is safe.

steps.prompt: Next day, Gauri asks quietly what she'd have to say if the counsellor talks to her. What do you suggest?

options.text: Say she'll need to explain everything about herself
options.then: She tenses. "I can't do that."

options.text: Say she only needs to share what happened to her
options.then: She relaxes a little. "Just what they did. Okay."

options.text: Offer to go in and answer for her instead
options.then: "I'd rather say it myself," she says.

options.text: Say she can just deny it all to avoid a fuss
options.then: "Then nothing changes," she says.

steps.why: Getting help never means sharing anything private. What happened is enough.

scenarios.debrief: If one adult won't act, try another. The person still deserves real help.
scenarios.relearn: If one adult brushes it off, calmly try another trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: A new classmate, Aisha, is being frozen out and whispered about for who she is.

options.text: Join the whispers so you stay in with the group
options.then: Aisha hears her name and looks away.

options.text: Smile at her from your usual table
options.then: She smiles back, but eats alone again.

options.text: Ask her straight out if the rumours are true
options.then: Aisha freezes. "What rumours?"

options.text: Sit with her and include her, simply and warmly
options.then: Aisha looks up, surprised. "Oh. Hi. Yes, please."

steps.why: Warm, simple inclusion tells her she belongs here.

steps.prompt: Later, your friends say Aisha is 'weird' and ask what you think. What do you say?

options.text: Agree she's a bit weird, to keep the peace
options.then: They laugh, and the whispers grow.

options.text: Say she's nice, and they should get to know her
options.then: One friend shrugs. "Maybe. She did look lonely."

options.text: Say you don't really know her, so no comment

options.text: Tell them they're all cruel and fake
options.then: They go quiet, and freeze you out for the afternoon.

options.then: She grins. "Yes! I'm good with posters."

scenarios.debrief: Warm, simple inclusion of someone left out for who they are is everyday dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Include the person left out; a warm welcome is quiet courage.

scenarios.hook: Some classmates keep tagging Kabir in cruel posts about who he is.

options.text: Reply to the bullies with something nastier

options.text: Scroll past so you don't feed the attention

options.text: Message Kabir that you're with him, and leave the post
options.then: Kabir replies "thanks". The post stays up and keeps spreading.

options.text: "Maybe post less about yourself for a while."

options.text: "That's not true. This is on them, not you."
options.then: Kabir's shoulders drop a little. "I needed to hear that," he says.

options.text: "Just ignore them. They'll get bored."
options.then: Kabir shrugs. "They haven't so far," he says, and changes the subject.

options.text: "Want me to find out who it is and expose them?"
options.then: Kabir looks worried. "Please don't. That'll make it worse."

steps.why: It is never his fault. Hiding who he is was never the fix.

steps.prompt: A week on, the posts keep coming from new accounts. What do you do?

options.text: Keep reporting each new account, just the two of you
options.then: Each account goes down, and a new one pops up a day later.

options.text: Tell Kabir to stay off his phone till it blows over
options.then: Kabir logs off. The posts carry on, and he hears about them at school.

options.text: Help Kabir block them and tell a teacher, with screenshots
options.then: Kabir picks his class teacher. She takes the screenshots and says she'll act.

options.text: Post a public callout naming who you think is behind it
options.then: The thread explodes into a fight, and Kabir's name is everywhere again.

steps.why: When it keeps going, a trusted adult can act in ways two students can't.

steps.prompt: Later, a classmate sends you a meme about Kabir to laugh at. What do you do?

options.text: Send back a laughing emoji to keep things easy
options.then: The classmate sends two more. Each one has Kabir's name on it.

options.text: Forward it to Kabir so he knows what's out there
options.then: Kabir sees it at midnight. He doesn't reply.

options.text: Don't pass it on, and report it
options.then: The meme is taken down by evening, and fewer people see it.

options.text: Delete it and say nothing
options.then: It's gone from your phone, but it's still going round everyone else's.

steps.why: Not passing it on and reporting it stops the pile-on instead of feeding it.

scenarios.debrief: For online identity abuse: report it, help them block, support the person and bring in a trusted adult.
scenarios.relearn: Help them report and block; remind them it isn't their fault.

scenarios.hook: After class, Meher tells you the bullying is so bad she feels there's no point going on.

options.text: Say it's not that deep, and she'll feel better tomorrow

options.text: Go and confront the bullies right away
options.then: Meher grabs your arm. "Please don't. Just stay."

options.text: Stay with her, and say you care and want to help
options.then: Meher's eyes fill. She stays beside you and starts to talk.

options.text: Give her some space and check in tomorrow
options.then: Meher picks up her bag and leaves alone. Her words stay with you all evening.

steps.prompt: Later, Meher texts asking you to promise not to tell anyone what she said. What do you reply?

options.text: "I promise. It stays between us."
options.then: Meher sends a heart. You're left holding something too heavy to carry alone.

options.text: "Okay, if you promise to cheer up."
options.then: Meher sends a smiley. You can tell she doesn't mean it.

options.text: Say yes now, then quietly tell a teacher later

options.text: "I care too much to keep this secret. Let's get help together."
options.then: Meher doesn't reply for a while. Then: "Okay. But stay with me?"

steps.prompt: That night, Meher messages again: "I can't stop feeling like there's no point." What do you do?

options.text: Get a parent, and stay on chat while she calls Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: Your mum sits with you while Meher calls. Later Meher texts: "They really listened."

options.text: Text her the Tele-MANAS number and say goodnight

options.text: Tell her to think about happier things and try to sleep

options.text: Leave it for tonight and see how she is at school
options.then: You put your phone away. Next morning, Meher looks like she hasn't slept.

steps.prompt: Next morning, the same bullies shove past Meher in the corridor. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to keep her head down so they lose interest
options.then: Meher spends the day trying to be invisible. It doesn't stop them.

options.text: Promise to walk with her between classes

options.text: Post about the bullies so the whole school knows

options.text: Go with her to the counsellor about all of it
options.then: The counsellor hears about the bullying and how low Meher feels, and makes a plan with her.

steps.why: A trusted adult can stop the bullying and help with how low she feels. None of it is Meher's fault.

steps.prompt: Back in class, a friend asks what's going on with Meher lately. What do you say?

options.text: "That's Meher's to share, not mine."
options.then: Your friend nods and drops it.

options.text: "She's being bullied and feels really low."
options.then: Your friend's eyes widen. By lunch, two more people are asking Meher about it.

options.text: "Ask Meher. She'll tell you."
options.then: Your friend does. Meher has to dodge questions she never wanted.

options.text: "She's kind of having a breakdown."
options.then: The word spreads fast. Meher hears it by the end of the day.

steps.why: What Meher is going through is hers to share. Keeping it private protects her.

scenarios.debrief: If a bullied friend is in distress, stay with them, don't keep it secret, and reach trusted support together.
scenarios.relearn: Distress needs care: stay, listen, and help them reach Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: In class today, a few students mocked Tanvi for who she is. You find her alone in the library.
scenarios.setup: You take the chair next to hers.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "It's fine. I'm used to it by now."

options.text: "Yeah, you'll get used to it eventually."
options.then: Tanvi gives a tight nod and turns back to her book.

options.text: "You shouldn't have to be. That wasn't okay."
options.then: Tanvi's voice wobbles. "It really wasn't, was it?"

options.text: "Good. Better not to let them see it hurts."
options.then: Tanvi shrugs. "Sure," she says, looking away.

options.text: "Want me to tell the whole class off tomorrow?"
options.then: Tanvi looks alarmed. "Please don't make it bigger."

steps.why: Nobody should have to get used to mockery. Saying it wasn't okay names the real problem.

steps.prompt: Tanvi asks: "Maybe if I changed how I dress, they'd stop?"

options.text: "Maybe, if it makes things easier for you."
options.then: Tanvi nods slowly. "I could try," she says flatly.

options.text: "Honestly, people would stop noticing you."
options.then: Tanvi's face closes. "So the problem's me."

options.text: "It's not your fault. You don't have to change for them."
options.then: Tanvi tugs at her sleeve, thinking. "I like how I dress."

options.text: "Don't worry about it. They'll get bored soon."
options.then: Tanvi shrugs. "And until then I just take it?"

steps.why: The bullying is the problem, not her. Saying so lifts blame she shouldn't carry.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says quietly: "I just don't want to sit alone tomorrow."

options.text: "Then sit with me. I'm with you."
options.then: Tanvi smiles properly for the first time today. "Okay."

options.text: "Maybe sit at the back, where they won't see you."
options.then: Tanvi nods. "I'll find a corner where nobody looks, then."

options.text: "I'd sit with you, but they might start on me too."
options.then: Tanvi looks away. "Yeah. I get it."

options.text: "You'll be fine. Just ignore them."
options.then: Tanvi nods, unconvinced, and stares down at the table.

steps.why: "I'm with you" means showing up, and sitting with her says it plainly.

steps.prompt: Tanvi admits: "It's not just today. They've been at it for weeks."

options.text: "Weeks? You should have told someone ages ago."
options.then: Tanvi flinches. "I'm telling you now, aren't I?"

options.text: "I'll keep it quiet. It's your business."
options.then: Tanvi looks relieved. The weeks of it carry on unseen.

options.text: "Let's get proof. I'll film them next time."
options.then: Tanvi shakes her head. "That'll just make them angrier."

options.text: "That's a lot to carry. Shall we tell Ms Rao together?"
options.then: Tanvi nods slowly. "If you come with me, yes."

steps.why: Weeks of bullying needs a trusted adult, and going together makes it easier to tell.

scenarios.relearn: Tell a bullied person: that wasn't okay, not your fault, I'm with you.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Dev keeps using an identity slur as a casual filler word.
scenarios.setup: On the walk home, he does it again.

steps.prompt: Dev laughs: "Bro, it's just a word. Everyone says it."

options.text: "Whatever. Say what you want."
options.then: Dev grins and says it again, then glances at you. "What, does that actually bug you?"

options.text: "Only an idiot would talk like that."
options.then: Dev's grin vanishes. "Wow. Okay, chill."

options.text: "It's a slur, though. Can you drop it?"
options.then: Dev pauses. "Wait, seriously? I never thought about it."

options.text: "Bro. Not cool."
options.then: Dev laughs. "What's not cool?" He moves on before you answer.

steps.why: Calling it a slur plainly, with a simple ask, lets him change without a fight.

steps.prompt: Dev adds: "I mean, nobody here is like that. Who's it hurting?"

options.text: "You don't know who's like that. Someone might be."
options.then: Dev looks around. "Wait, who? Are you saying someone is?"

options.text: "It's about respect, not who's listening."
options.then: Dev frowns, thinking. "Huh. Fair enough."

options.text: "True. Then it doesn't really matter."
options.then: Dev nods. Then he squints at you. "You still look bothered, though."

options.text: "Wow. Only a bigot would say that."
options.then: Dev stops walking. "That's a lot, man."

steps.why: Respect isn't only for when someone's listening, and it never means guessing about anyone.

steps.prompt: Dev asks: "So what do you actually want? It slips out without me thinking."

options.text: "If it slips out again, we're done."
options.then: Dev raises his eyebrows. "Over one word? Okay."

options.text: "Okay, forget I said anything."
options.then: Dev shrugs. Next day the word is back, and you let it go.

options.text: "I'll tell the coach if you say it again."
options.then: Dev bristles. "Seriously? You'd report me?"

options.text: "Just try. I'll nudge you when it does."
options.then: Dev laughs. "Deal. Just not in front of everyone."

steps.why: A friendly nudge helps a habit change, and keeps the friendship too.

scenarios.relearn: Identity slurs aren't filler; calmly ask a friend to drop them.

scenarios.hook: Pari, a junior in your dance club, is teased about who she is and asks what to do.

options.text: "Maybe, if it makes life easier."
options.then: Pari nods sadly. "I'll tell them next week."

options.text: "No. You belong here, and it's not your fault."
options.then: Pari looks up. "You really think I belong?"

options.text: "Just toughen up and ignore them."

options.text: "Quit? Over some teasing? Come on, don't be silly."
options.then: Pari's face goes red. "It's not just some teasing."

steps.why: She shouldn't have to give up what she loves. The teasing is the problem, not her.

steps.prompt: Pari adds quietly: "The others in the club never say anything."

options.text: "They probably agree with them, honestly."
options.then: Pari's eyes fill. "So everyone thinks it."

options.text: "Then try to fit in more with the group."
options.then: Pari looks at her shoes. "I don't know how to be different."

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll shout at them at practice tomorrow."
options.then: Pari looks scared. "Then they'll know I told you."

options.text: "That doesn't make them right. You deserve respect."
options.then: Pari straightens a little. "Okay. That helps."

steps.why: Others staying quiet doesn't make the teasing right. She deserves respect regardless.

steps.prompt: Pari asks: "Who could actually make it stop?"

options.text: "Let's tell Mrs Kaur together after practice."
options.then: Pari takes a breath. "Okay. If you come too."

options.text: "Nobody, really. It'll stop when they're bored."
options.then: Pari's shoulders slump. "So I just wait."

options.text: "I'll tell Mrs Kaur for you. You don't need to come."
options.then: Pari hesitates. "Will they ask me about it anyway?"

options.text: "Post about it, so everyone sees what they do."
options.then: Pari's eyes widen. "Then everyone will talk about me."

steps.why: Telling a trusted teacher together gets real help, and Pari keeps a say in it.

scenarios.relearn: Guide a teased junior: not your fault, you deserve respect, and let's tell an adult.

scenarios.hook: Your friends are laughing at a 'banter' clip that mocks Nikhil for who he is.
scenarios.setup: At lunch, Arjun holds his phone out to you.

steps.prompt: Arjun says: "Watch this. It's just banter. He won't even see it."

options.text: "Haha. Send it to me."
options.then: Arjun sends it. Now it's on your phone too.

options.text: "You're all disgusting for laughing at this."
options.then: The table goes silent. Arjun rolls his eyes. "Relax. It's a joke."

options.text: "It's mocking who he is. I'll pass."
options.then: Arjun's grin fades a little. "Okay, okay. It's just a clip."

options.text: "Nah, not in the mood."
options.then: Arjun shrugs and shows it to the next person.

steps.why: Naming that it mocks who he is, without attacking anyone, is calm and clear.

steps.prompt: Arjun says: "It's going round every group. I'm sending it to the class one too."

options.text: "Whatever. Just don't expect me to laugh."
options.then: Arjun shrugs and forwards it to the class group.

options.text: "Don't. It hurts him. Let's not send it further."
options.then: Arjun looks at the screen, then puts his phone down. "Fine."

options.text: "Yeah, okay. One more forward won't hurt."
options.then: The clip lands in a group of a hundred people.

options.text: "Who made it? Let's find them and make one back."
options.then: Arjun laughs. "A revenge clip? That would go viral."

steps.why: Asking him not to forward it keeps it from reaching more people.

steps.prompt: Later, Arjun asks: "Do you think Nikhil's seen it?"

options.text: "Probably. Doesn't matter. It's just a clip."
options.then: Arjun shrugs. "Yeah. Guess so."

options.text: "Let's DM him and say it was all a joke."
options.then: Arjun types it out. "Hope he doesn't take it badly."

options.text: "Maybe. I'll check on him and tell a teacher."
options.then: Arjun nods slowly. "Yeah. Okay. That makes sense."

options.text: "I'll check on him. No need to involve teachers."
options.then: Arjun nods. The clip keeps moving from group to group.

steps.why: Checking on Nikhil and telling an adult helps him, and helps stop the clip spreading.

steps.prompt: Next day, Arjun admits: "I'd already sent that clip to three groups."

options.text: "Too late now. Forget it."
options.then: Arjun shrugs, relieved. The clip keeps circulating.

options.text: "Wow. You're as bad as whoever made it."
options.then: Arjun's face drops. "I was trying to tell you."

options.text: "Ask them to delete it. And maybe say sorry to Nikhil."
options.then: Arjun rubs his neck. "Yeah. I can do that."

options.text: "Just delete it from your phone. Done."
options.then: Arjun deletes it. The copies he sent are still out there.

steps.why: Owning it means pulling it back and making it right with Nikhil, not only deleting.

scenarios.relearn: Name identity-targeting 'banter' calmly; don't pass the clip on.

scenarios.hook: For a week, the class has frozen Farhan out for who he is. Today he's eating alone.
scenarios.setup: You walk over with your tiffin.

steps.prompt: Farhan looks up and asks: "Did someone send you over?"

options.text: "People are being so weird about you, huh?"
options.then: Farhan's face closes. "Yeah. I noticed."

options.text: "I just felt really bad seeing you alone."
options.then: Farhan stiffens. "I'm fine on my own, thanks."

options.text: "Nope. Just wanted company. Mind if I sit?"
options.then: Farhan moves his bag. "Sure. It is quieter here."

options.text: "No. Come sit with my group. They'll be fine."
options.then: Farhan glances over. "They're the ones who stopped talking to me."

steps.why: A simple, easy welcome includes him without making him the topic.

steps.prompt: Farhan says: "You know people might start talking about you too."

options.text: "Let them. I like sitting here."
options.then: Farhan laughs, surprised. "Okay. Pass the pickle, then."

options.text: "Why? What did you do to them?"
options.then: Farhan pushes his tiffin away. "Nothing. That's the point."

options.text: "True. Let's move somewhere less visible."
options.then: Farhan picks up his tiffin, but his smile has gone.

options.text: "Yeah. Maybe I'll just sit here today, then."
options.then: Farhan nods. "Today. Got it."

steps.why: Staying, simply and without fuss, shows him he's worth sitting with.

steps.prompt: Farhan says quietly: "Someone wrote something about me on my desk today."

options.text: "Just rub it off quickly, before anyone else sees."
options.then: Farhan nods. The words are gone, but he stays quiet all lunch.

options.text: "Ugh, that's awful. Who do you think did it?"
options.then: Farhan shrugs. "Does it matter? It'll happen again."

options.text: "That's not okay, and not your fault. Tell Ms Thomas with me?"
options.then: Farhan hesitates, then nods. "After lunch. If you come."

options.text: "I'll find out who did it and tell them off myself."
options.then: Farhan looks alarmed. "Please don't. That'll make it worse."

steps.why: It's never his fault. A trusted teacher can stop it, and going together makes telling easier.

steps.prompt: The next day, Farhan asks: "Are you sitting here again?"

options.text: "Maybe not today. My friends are asking questions."
options.then: Farhan nods and looks down at his lunch.

options.text: "Sure, but let's not make it a thing, okay?"
options.then: Farhan's smile falters. "Okay. I won't."

options.text: "Yes. And I'll tell everyone to stop being horrible."
options.then: Farhan looks worried. "Please don't announce it."

options.text: "If you'll have me. Want to do the bio notes too?"
options.then: Farhan grins and pulls out his notebook.

steps.why: Ordinary, steady company, day after day, is what inclusion really looks like.

scenarios.relearn: A simple, warm 'mind if I sit?' is inclusion in action.

scenarios.hook: Last week you laughed along when friends mocked Sana for who she is. Today you want to own it.
scenarios.setup: You find her alone by the water cooler.

steps.prompt: Sana asks warily: "What do you want?"

options.text: "Just wanted to say it was only a joke."
options.then: Sana's face hardens. "It didn't feel like one."

options.text: "I laughed along last week. I'm sorry."
options.then: Sana folds her arms. "Okay. I didn't expect that."

options.text: "Sorry if you got upset about last week."
options.then: Sana raises an eyebrow. "If I got upset?"

options.text: "Nothing much. How was the test?"
options.then: Sana shrugs. "Fine. But that's not why you're here, is it?"

steps.why: A plain apology names what you did, with no excuses, so it can land.

steps.prompt: Sana asks: "Last week you laughed with them. Why come to me now?"

options.text: "I don't want people thinking I'm like them."
options.then: Sana snorts. "So this is about you."

options.text: "My mum said I should apologise."
options.then: Sana shrugs. "Tell her you did, then."

options.text: "Everyone was doing it. I just went along."
options.then: Sana sighs. "Yeah. Everyone always does."

options.text: "Because it hurt you, and I was part of it."
options.then: Sana looks at you for a long moment. "Thanks for saying that."

steps.why: Owning your part, without hiding behind the group, makes it real.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "They'll probably do it again tomorrow."

options.text: "I won't join in. If it keeps up, let's tell Sir."
options.then: Sana studies your face. "We'll see." Her voice is softer.

options.text: "Not my problem after today, though."
options.then: Sana nods slowly, like she expected that.

options.text: "Want me to fight them for you next time?"
options.then: Sana steps back. "No. I want them to stop."

options.text: "I'll just stay out of it from now on. That's fair."
options.then: "Staying out is what you did last time," Sana says.

steps.why: Making it right means choosing respect next time, and getting an adult if it goes on.

steps.prompt: At lunch, your friend Vikram asks: "What were you and Sana talking about?"

options.text: "Last week. Laughing along was wrong of me."
options.then: Vikram shrugs. "Huh. Okay." He doesn't laugh about it again.

options.text: "Nothing much. Just school stuff."
options.then: Vikram nods. Next time the group starts, he expects you to laugh.

options.text: "Relax. I was just keeping her quiet."
options.then: Vikram grins. Now the whole thing is a joke at Sana's expense.

options.text: "You should apologise to her too, or you're a coward."
options.then: Vikram scowls. "Back off. It was a joke."

steps.why: Saying plainly that it was wrong shows others that respect is something anyone can choose.

scenarios.relearn: Owning a mistake plainly, no excuses, is how you make it right.

scenarios.hook: You stood up for Aarav when he was mocked for who he is. Now Kunal wants to know why.
scenarios.setup: Kunal falls into step with you after class.

steps.prompt: Kunal asks: "Why'd you even bother? He's not your friend."

options.text: "No reason. I just felt like it."
options.then: Kunal shrugs. "Weird. Okay."

options.text: "Because those guys are total losers."
options.then: Kunal laughs. "So it was about them, not him."

options.text: "Everyone deserves to feel safe here. Him too."
options.then: Kunal thinks about it. "Huh. Never looked at it like that."

options.text: "Because no teachers were around to do it."
options.then: Kunal nods. "So if a teacher was there, you'd skip it?"

steps.why: The reason is simple: dignity and safety are for everyone, friend or not.

steps.prompt: Kunal asks: "Didn't you worry they'd come after you next?"

options.text: "Nope. I'd have fought all of them."
options.then: Kunal whistles. "Bold. There were four of them."

options.text: "A bit. So I'd only do it when my friends back me."
options.then: Kunal nods. "And if they're not around?"

options.text: "A bit. That's why I kept it calm and short."
options.then: Kunal nods. "Yeah. You didn't make a big scene."

options.text: "Yes. Next time I'll just stay out of it."
options.then: Kunal nods. "Makes sense," he says.

steps.why: Calm, short upstanding keeps you safe while still standing with him.

steps.prompt: Kunal asks: "What if it ever got really bad, like a fight?"

options.text: "Then I'd jump in. Someone has to."
options.then: Kunal looks doubtful. "Then there are two of you getting hurt."

options.text: "Then I'd film it, so there's proof."
options.then: "And it ends up everywhere," Kunal says. "Aarav would hate that."

options.text: "Then I'd call Aarav's friends to come and help."
options.then: Kunal tilts his head. "And if they're not around either?"

options.text: "Then I'd get a teacher and stay with Aarav."
options.then: Kunal nods. "That actually sounds doable."

steps.why: When it could turn unsafe, getting an adult and staying with him is the safe courage.

scenarios.relearn: Standing up for dignity is for a simple reason: everyone deserves to feel safe.

scenarios.hook: For weeks, Yash in your class has been bullied for who he is. You decide to tell Mrs Menon.
scenarios.setup: You wait until the staffroom is nearly empty.

steps.prompt: Mrs Menon asks: "Yes? Is everything all right?"

options.text: "Actually, never mind. It's probably nothing."
options.then: She looks at you a moment longer. "You came for a reason. Go on."

options.text: "Ma'am, can we talk privately? It's about bullying."
options.then: She puts down her pen. "Of course. Sit. Tell me."

options.text: "Ma'am, the whole class is bullying Yash!"
options.then: Two teachers look up. Mrs Menon lowers her voice. "Quietly, please."

options.text: "Ma'am, is there a school rule about teasing?"
options.then: "There is," she says. "Why do you ask?"

steps.why: Asking for a private word makes it easy for her to listen properly.

steps.prompt: Mrs Menon asks: "Take your time. What's been happening?"

options.text: "It's Yash. But I can't say who's doing it."
options.then: She frowns gently. "I'll try, but it's hard to stop without knowing who."

options.text: "Everyone says Yash is, you know, different."
options.then: Mrs Menon holds up a hand. "Let's keep to what happened, not guesses."

options.text: "Yash gets mocked every day. I can tell you what I saw."
options.then: She listens and writes down what you describe.

options.text: "Rahul's gang picks on Yash. They're horrible people."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Tell me what they did, not what they are."

steps.why: Sticking to what you saw, with no guesses about Yash, gives her what she needs to act.

steps.prompt: Mrs Menon says: "I'll look into this. How is Yash doing right now?"

options.text: "He's fine. He's used to it."
options.then: Mrs Menon frowns. "No one should have to be."

options.text: "Please don't talk to him. He'll know I told."
options.then: She pauses. "I'll be careful, but I do need to check on him."

options.text: "I don't know. That's his problem, really."
options.then: She looks at you quietly. "It's all of ours."

options.text: "He seems low. Could you check on him gently?"
options.then: She nods. "I'll find a quiet moment with him today."

steps.why: Pointing her to Yash quietly means he gets support, not only the bullies stopped.

steps.prompt: Back in class, your friend Neha asks: "Why were you in the staffroom so long?"

options.text: "Reported Yash's bullies. Don't tell anyone."
options.then: Neha's eyes widen. By sixth period, half the class knows.

options.text: "Had to ask Ma'am something. Lunch?"
options.then: Neha shrugs. "Sure. I'm starving."

options.text: "Telling Ma'am about Yash. You know, his thing."
options.then: Neha leans in. "His thing? What thing?"

options.text: "Can't say. It's a big secret."
options.then: Neha's curiosity spikes. "Ooh. Now you have to tell me."

steps.why: Keeping it low-key protects Yash, and stops the report becoming gossip.

scenarios.relearn: You can report bullying quietly and clearly to a trusted teacher.

scenarios.hook: Neel in your class is bullied for who he is, and your friend Riya has a theory about why.
scenarios.setup: You're both waiting for the school bus.

steps.prompt: Riya says: "Honestly, if he just blended in, they'd leave him alone."

options.text: "Yeah, maybe he should tone it down."
options.then: Riya nods. "Right? It's just common sense."

options.text: "No one earns bullying by being themselves."
options.then: Riya tilts her head. "Sure, but he does make it easy for them."

options.text: "That's such a disgusting thing to say."
options.then: Riya flushes. "Wow. I was just saying."

options.text: "Maybe. But it's still mean of them."
options.then: Riya shrugs. "Mean, sure. But he's asking for it."

steps.why: Being himself isn't the problem. Saying so plainly puts the blame where it belongs.

steps.prompt: Riya adds: "He dresses so differently. He must know people will react."

options.text: "True. He could make it easier on himself."
options.then: Riya nods, satisfied, and checks her phone.

options.text: "Maybe he dresses like that because he's, you know..."
options.then: Riya's eyes widen. "Ooh. Should I ask around?"

options.text: "Dressing how he likes isn't permission to bully him."
options.then: Riya pauses. "Okay. That does sound unfair when you say it."

options.text: "Anyway, let's not talk about Neel."
options.then: Riya shrugs. The idea stays exactly where it was.

steps.why: The bullies choose to bully. What he wears never makes it his fault.

steps.prompt: On the bus, two boys start mocking Neel. Riya whispers: "Not again. Do we just sit down?"

options.text: "Yes. Just sit down. It's not our business."
options.then: Riya slides into a seat, relieved. Behind you, the laughing goes on.

options.text: "Film it, so the school has proof later."
options.then: Your phone goes up. Neel sees it, and his face drops even further.

options.text: "Let's sit by Neel. That's all he needs."
options.then: Neel looks up, grateful. The boys keep at it all the way to school.

options.text: "Let's sit by Neel, and tell the teacher up front."
options.then: Neel looks up, relieved. The teacher walks back, and the boys go quiet.

steps.why: Siding with Neel and telling a teacher gets him help safely. Being himself is never his fault.

scenarios.relearn: No one earns bullying by being themselves; the bullying is the problem.

scenarios.hook: Late one night, your friend Aditya texts that he feels low and has no one to talk to.

steps.prompt: His message ends with "sorry for dumping this on you". What do you reply?

options.text: "Just cheer up, man. Sleep it off."
options.then: Aditya sends a thumbs up and goes offline.

options.text: "Bro, it's 1 am. Can we talk tomorrow?"
options.then: "Sure," Aditya replies. He doesn't message the next day.

options.text: "Don't be sorry. I'm here. Want to talk?"
options.then: Aditya replies fast. "Yeah. Thanks. It's been a rough few weeks."

options.text: "Same. Everyone feels like that sometimes."
options.then: "Yeah," Aditya writes, and the chat goes quiet.

steps.why: Saying you're there, without brushing it off, lets him keep talking.

steps.prompt: When you next talk, Aditya says he doesn't want to burden his parents. What do you suggest?

options.text: Tele-MANAS 14416, and you'll stay on chat while he calls
options.then: Aditya calls. Later he texts: "That helped. They were kind."

options.text: Searching online for ways to stop feeling low
options.then: Aditya finds a dozen lists. None of them feels like a real person.

options.text: Keeping busy with games until the feeling passes
options.then: Aditya tries a game, then another. The feeling stays.

options.text: Talking only to you about it, every single night
options.then: Aditya agrees. You feel the weight of being his only person.

steps.why: A trained listener plus your company is real support he can reach right away.

steps.prompt: A week later, Aditya still feels low most days. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him it's probably just a phase
options.then: Aditya stops bringing it up. You can't tell if he's better.

options.text: Offer to go with him to the school counsellor
options.then: Aditya agrees to go on Monday. He asks you to wait outside.

options.text: Stop asking. He'll bring it up if he wants to
options.then: Days pass. Aditya doesn't bring it up, and neither do you.

options.text: Send him a long list of mood-boosting tips
options.then: Aditya replies "thx". He doesn't open the link.

steps.why: When low days keep coming, a counsellor or trusted adult can help in ways a friend can't.

scenarios.debrief: When a friend feels low, your company and a real helpline do far more than 'cheer up'.
scenarios.relearn: A real number plus your company beats brushing a friend off.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Mira hints that things are tense at home because of who she is.

options.then: Mira clams up. "It's nothing. Forget it."

options.text: Tell her families always come round in the end

options.text: Say she should stand up to her parents tonight

steps.prompt: At lunch, a classmate asks why Mira has been so quiet lately. What do you say?

options.then: By evening, three people are whispering about Mira's home.

options.text: Hint that it's to do with who she is
options.then: The classmate's eyes widen. You can see the guessing start.

options.text: Say you can't say, because it's private stuff
options.then: The classmate's curiosity sharpens. "Private like what?"

options.text: Shrug, and suggest they sit with Mira at lunch
options.then: The classmate nods and sits with Mira. Her story stays hers.

steps.why: What Mira shared is hers alone. Keeping it private is how you never out anyone.

steps.prompt: A week later, Mira says things at home are getting harder and she feels stuck. What do you do?

options.text: Mention a counsellor or Tele-MANAS 14416, both private
options.then: Mira saves the number. "I didn't know I could call without anyone knowing."

options.text: Tell her to keep her head down until she's older
options.then: Mira nods. She seems to fold a little further into herself.

options.text: Offer to go and speak to her parents yourself
options.then: Mira looks alarmed. "Please don't. It'll get so much worse."

options.text: Promise you'll be the only one she ever needs
options.then: Mira smiles weakly. You both know you can't fix this alone.

steps.why: Nothing is wrong with who she is. A counsellor or private line can help, at her pace.

scenarios.debrief: Mira isn't the problem. Listen, keep her confidence unless she's unsafe, and point her to private support.
scenarios.relearn: Listen, keep confidence, and point to a confidential route; never broadcast it.

scenarios.hook: Ayaan, the nine-year-old next door, has seemed scared to go home lately.

steps.prompt: Tonight he's sitting on your building's steps long after dark. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him to head home before his family worries
options.then: Ayaan stands up slowly. He looks back twice.

options.text: Sit with him and gently ask if he's okay
options.then: Ayaan shrugs, then says quietly, "Not really."

options.text: Leave him be. Kids sulk sometimes
options.then: Ayaan stays on the step a while. Later you hear his door bang.

options.text: Ask him lots of questions about what happens at home
options.then: Ayaan shrinks back. "Nothing. I'm fine."

steps.why: Calm company and one gentle question give him room to speak.

steps.prompt: A day later, Ayaan whispers that someone at home hurts him. What do you say?

options.text: "Who? What exactly did they do to you?"
options.then: Ayaan goes quiet and stares at the ground. "Forget it."

options.text: "Are you sure? Maybe you misunderstood."
options.then: Ayaan's face falls. "I knew you wouldn't believe me. Don't tell anyone."

options.text: "I'm glad you told me. This is not your fault."
options.then: Ayaan's lip trembles, but he nods and stays beside you.

options.text: "That's awful. I'm going over there right now."
options.then: Ayaan panics and grabs your sleeve. "No! Please don't."

steps.why: Believing him and saying it's not his fault, without questions, helps him feel safe.

steps.prompt: Ayaan begs you not to tell anyone, or he'll be in trouble. What do you say?

options.text: "Okay. It stays between us, I promise."
options.then: Ayaan nods. You go home knowing he's still not safe.

options.text: "You won't be in trouble. I'll sort it out myself."
options.then: Ayaan looks hopeful. You realise you have no idea how.

options.text: "I can't keep this secret. I'll get help to keep you safe."
options.then: Ayaan looks scared, but he holds your hand a little tighter.

options.text: "Okay, if you promise to tell me if it happens again."
options.then: Ayaan promises. For now, no adult knows he's unsafe.

steps.why: A secret that keeps a child unsafe is an unsafe secret. Telling is how he gets protected.

steps.prompt: That night, you hear loud shouting from Ayaan's house. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a trusted adult right away and call Childline 1098
options.then: Your aunt takes it seriously and calls with you. Childline says they'll follow up.

options.text: Go over and confront the adult yourself
options.then: At the door your heart pounds. Facing an angry adult alone could make it worse.

options.text: Wait to see if it happens again before you act
options.then: The house goes quiet. You lie awake, not knowing if Ayaan is okay.

options.text: Message your friends to ask what they'd do
options.then: Your friends reply with ideas, but still no adult knows about Ayaan.

steps.why: An adult and Childline 1098 can protect him. You don't have to carry this alone.

steps.prompt: The next day, Ayaan asks if he's in trouble for telling. What do you say?

options.text: "Maybe a bit. You should have told someone sooner."
options.then: Ayaan's eyes fill. "I was scared," he says.

options.text: "No. Telling was okay, and none of it is your fault."
options.then: Ayaan looks at you for a long moment, then nods.

options.text: "Let's not talk about it anymore, okay?"
options.then: Ayaan goes quiet. He still doesn't know if he did something wrong.

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll make sure nothing bad ever happens."
options.then: Ayaan brightens. You hope you can keep a promise that big.

steps.why: He needs to hear clearly that telling was okay and that none of it is his fault.

scenarios.debrief: Believe the child, get an adult and Childline 1098, and never carry danger alone.
scenarios.relearn: For a child at risk, get an adult and Childline 1098. Don't carry danger alone.

scenarios.hook: Earlier, your friend Leela used an outdated word for someone, and they looked hurt.
scenarios.setup: She brings it up on the way to class.

steps.prompt: Leela says: "I didn't know the right word. I feel so stupid."

options.text: "Honestly, you should have known by now."
options.then: Leela's face falls. "Great. Now I feel worse."

options.text: "It's fine. Words don't matter that much anyway."
options.then: Leela looks unsure. "It seemed to matter to her."

options.text: "No worries. You can just ask what people prefer."
options.then: Leela lets out a breath. "I didn't think I was allowed to ask."

options.text: "Yeah, that was pretty awkward to watch."
options.then: Leela groans. "Thanks. I'll never say anything again."

steps.why: Not knowing a word is okay. Asking what people prefer is all respect needs.

steps.prompt: Leela asks: "Should I say sorry, or will that make it weirder?"

options.text: "A quick sorry, then use her word. No fuss."
options.then: Leela nods. "Short and simple. I can do that."

options.text: "Don't. Just pretend it never happened."
options.then: Leela nods, but she still winces every time she sees her.

options.text: "Write her a long apology letter tonight."
options.then: Leela starts drafting. It's two pages by nine o'clock.

options.text: "Say sorry in front of everyone, so it counts."
options.then: Leela looks horrified. "That would make it all about me."

steps.why: A short apology and the right word fix it without making it a big moment.

steps.prompt: Leela asks: "But what if I get it wrong again someday?"

options.text: "Then avoid talking about people like that."
options.then: Leela frowns. "That sounds lonelier, not better."

options.text: "You won't. Just memorise all the terms tonight."
options.then: Leela sighs. "There are so many, though."

options.text: "Then just don't care what anyone thinks of you."
options.then: Leela shrugs. "I do care, though. That's the point."

options.text: "Then you say sorry and keep learning. Everyone does."
options.then: Leela smiles a little. "Okay. That feels less scary."

steps.why: Mistakes happen. Owning them kindly and learning is what respect looks like over time.

scenarios.relearn: It's fine not to know a word; just ask people what they prefer.

options.text: "Good idea. Then we'll all know for sure."

options.text: "Don't. It's his to share, if he ever wants to."

options.then: Ritika shrugs and walks over to him alone.
