steps.prompt: Tushar asks: "So why is everyone suddenly talking about it?"

options.text: "Because it's trendy. You're kind of right."
options.then: Tushar grins. "Told you."

options.text: "Because people just copy each other online."
options.then: Tushar nods. "So it does spread."

options.text: "More people feel safe to be open now."
options.then: Tushar thinks. "Huh. That makes sense, actually."

options.text: "No idea. It just is like that now."
options.then: Tushar shrugs. "Sounds like a fad to me."

steps.why: Being talked about more isn't the same as being new. People simply feel safer to speak.

steps.prompt: Tushar says: "Anyway, it'll probably all die down in a few years."

options.text: "Maybe. Most things do, eventually."
options.then: Tushar nods. "Yeah. Let it run its course."

options.text: "Ugh. You're impossible to talk to."
options.then: Tushar shrugs. "Just saying what I think."

options.text: "Let's just agree to disagree on this one, okay?"
options.then: Tushar nods. The 'fad' idea is still sitting there.

options.text: "People aren't trends. They'll still be here."
options.then: Tushar laughs. "Fair. That was a weird thing to say."

steps.why: Who people are isn't a trend. It was here before, and it will stay.

scenarios.relearn: Correct 'it's a fad' kindly: it's longstanding across history and India's own traditions.

scenarios.hook: After football, your teammate Kartik grumbles about a school talk on respecting everyone.
scenarios.setup: You're both catching your breath on the sideline.

steps.prompt: Kartik asks: "Seriously, why should I respect people so different from me?"

options.text: "Yeah, why bother, honestly?"
options.then: Kartik nods. "Exactly. Not my problem."

options.text: "Because you'll get in trouble at school if you don't."
options.then: Kartik smirks. "So only when teachers are watching."

options.text: "You don't have to be like someone to respect them."
options.then: Kartik frowns. "Hm. I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: "Because you're a bad person if you don't."
options.then: Kartik's jaw sets. "Oh, so now I'm the bad guy."

steps.why: Respect doesn't need sameness. It's owed to everyone.

steps.prompt: Kartik says: "Honestly, half that talk went over my head."

options.text: "Then just keep away from them. Simple."
options.then: Kartik nods. "That's what I've been doing."

options.text: "You don't need to get it all. Just be decent."
options.then: Kartik shrugs. "Decent. I can probably manage that."

options.text: "You should understand by now. It's not hard."
options.then: Kartik bristles. "It is for me."

options.text: "Then learn everything about them first."
options.then: Kartik groans. "Sounds like a whole course."

steps.why: Understanding can grow later. Treating people decently doesn't have to wait.

steps.prompt: Kartik asks: "And if I don't agree with how they live?"

options.text: "Then you can say whatever you like about them."
options.then: Kartik grins. "Good to know."

options.text: "Then honestly, you're the problem here."
options.then: Kartik turns away. "Forget I asked."

options.text: "You can disagree and still treat them with dignity."
options.then: Kartik nods slowly. "Okay. Disagree, but no being a jerk."

options.text: "Then just keep quiet about it forever."
options.then: Kartik shrugs. "So I just hide what I think?"

steps.why: You can hold different beliefs and still give everyone dignity. That part isn't up for debate.

scenarios.relearn: You don't have to be like someone to treat them with respect.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Ruhi has just shared something about who she is, and now she looks nervous.
scenarios.setup: She's waiting for you to say something.

steps.prompt: Ruhi asks quietly: "So... are we okay?"

options.text: "Whoa. Okay. That's a lot to take in."
options.then: Ruhi's smile flickers. "Sorry. I didn't mean to dump it on you."

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. Nothing changes. We're good."
options.then: Ruhi laughs with relief. "I've been scared to say it for months."

options.text: "Honestly, I kind of always knew, you know."
options.then: Ruhi freezes. "Knew? Is it that obvious?"

options.text: "Of course we are! So, does anyone else know about it yet?"
options.then: Ruhi tenses. "No. Why, should they?"

steps.why: Warm thanks and an unchanged friendship are what she needed to hear first.

steps.prompt: Ruhi says: "Do you have any questions? You can ask."

options.text: "So when did you decide?"
options.then: Ruhi's smile fades. "It's not really a decision."

options.text: "Are you sure it's not just a phase?"
options.then: Ruhi looks hurt. "I've thought about it for a long time."

options.text: "Just one. How can I be a good friend about it?"
options.then: Ruhi smiles. "Honestly? Just this. Exactly this."

options.text: "Loads. Tell me absolutely everything, from the start."
options.then: Ruhi hesitates. "Maybe not everything right now."

steps.why: Asking how to support her keeps the focus on her, not on prying.

steps.prompt: Ruhi says: "I'm not ready for anyone else to know yet."

options.text: "Not even Priya? She'd be so cool about it."
options.then: Ruhi's face tightens. "Not yet. Please."

options.text: "They won't hear it from me. It's yours to share."
options.then: Ruhi lets out a long breath. "Thank you. Really."

options.text: "You should tell people soon. It'll feel freeing."
options.then: Ruhi looks away. "Maybe. Not now."

options.text: "Okay. But people will probably guess anyway."
options.then: Ruhi's shoulders rise. "Do you think so?"

steps.why: Whether and when she tells anyone is entirely her choice.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Ruhi sighs: "My cousin says it's probably just a phase."

options.text: "Maybe she's right. Time will tell."
options.then: Ruhi's face falls. "You too?"

options.text: "Your cousin sounds really ignorant."
options.then: Ruhi winces. "She's not a bad person."

options.text: "That's not hers to decide. You know yourself."
options.then: Ruhi smiles a little. "I needed someone to say that."

options.text: "Don't listen to anyone. Just ignore it completely."
options.then: Ruhi nods, but the word 'phase' stays with her.

steps.why: It isn't anyone else's to dismiss or time. Ruhi knows herself best.

scenarios.relearn: Meet someone sharing with warmth and unchanged respect; nothing about your friendship changes.

scenarios.hook: Your grandfather uses an old, insulting label for a group, not realising it hurts.
scenarios.setup: You're watching the news together.

steps.prompt: Nanaji uses the label again and asks: "Why are they always on the news?"

options.text: "No idea. They just are these days."
options.then: Nanaji nods and keeps using the word.

options.text: "That word hurts, Nanaji. People use their own terms now."
options.then: Nanaji blinks. "Hurts? I didn't know that."

options.text: "Nanaji! You can't say that. It's so offensive."
options.then: Nanaji looks startled, then hurt. "I didn't mean anything."

options.text: "Ha, Nanaji, you're so old-fashioned."
options.then: Nanaji chuckles. "Old and proud." He says the word again.

steps.why: A gentle nudge, without shaming, helps him update an old habit.

steps.prompt: Nanaji says: "In my day, nobody talked about any of this."

options.text: "Your day was pretty backward, Nanaji."
options.then: Nanaji's face falls. "Was it?" he says quietly.

options.text: "I know. And the words we use have changed too."
options.then: Nanaji considers this. "Hm. Many things have changed."

options.text: "True. Things were simpler back then."
options.then: Nanaji nods, pleased, and uses the old word again.

options.text: "Doesn't matter now. Just stop saying that word."
options.then: Nanaji frowns. "Don't order me around."

steps.why: Respecting where he's coming from makes it easier for him to change the word.

steps.prompt: Later, a cousin corrects Nanaji's word, and he turns to you: "So what do people say now?"

options.text: "Just don't talk about them at all."
options.then: Nanaji shrugs. "Easier, I suppose."

options.text: "Look it up yourself, Nanaji."
options.then: Nanaji sighs. "You know I can't work that phone."

options.text: "Whatever sounds polite to you. You'll figure it out."
options.then: Nanaji frowns. "That's not much help."

options.text: "The words people use for themselves. I'll show you."
options.then: Nanaji hands you his reading glasses. "Go on, then."

steps.why: Using people's own words is the simple rule, and showing him makes it easy.

scenarios.relearn: Gently point out that an old label hurts; people use their own terms now.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin Mishti, who's eleven, heard the word 'spectrum' at school.
scenarios.setup: She finds you in the kitchen.

steps.prompt: Mishti asks: "What does 'the spectrum' even mean?"

options.text: "You're too young to ask that."
options.then: Mishti frowns. "Everyone keeps saying that."

options.text: "It's a long story. Go and ask your mum."
options.then: Mishti sighs. "She said to ask you."

options.text: "People vary in who they are and who they love."
options.then: Mishti thinks. "Like how some people are tall and some aren't?"

options.text: "It's some complicated thing from the internet."
options.then: Mishti looks more confused. "Is it bad?"

steps.why: A plain, honest answer for her age is clearer than dodging.

steps.prompt: Mishti asks: "Is it new? I never heard of it before."

options.text: "No. People have always been this way, everywhere."
options.then: Mishti nods. "Even in old times?"

options.text: "Yes, it's a pretty new thing, actually."
options.then: Mishti nods. "So it might go away."

options.text: "It's mostly in other countries, not here."
options.then: Mishti looks puzzled. "Not here?"

options.text: "Who knows? Doesn't really matter, does it?"
options.then: Mishti shrugs, still unsure.

steps.why: This variety isn't new. It's been part of people everywhere, including India.

steps.prompt: Mishti says: "A boy in my class said it's weird."

options.text: "Some people think so. Just stay out of it."
options.then: Mishti nods, unsure what to say next time.

options.text: "That boy sounds horrible."
options.then: Mishti frowns. "He's my friend, though."

options.text: "It's not weird. Everyone deserves kindness."
options.then: Mishti smiles. "That's what I told him!"

options.text: "Well, it is a bit different, isn't it?"
options.then: Mishti looks thoughtful. "So he's right?"

steps.why: Different isn't weird. Kindness and respect are for everyone.

scenarios.relearn: The spectrum just means people vary in who they are and who they love.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Om wants to learn more about identity but worries asking questions is rude.
scenarios.setup: He brings it up as you walk home.

steps.prompt: Om asks: "Is it rude to ask questions when someone talks about who they are?"

options.text: "Yes. Don't ask anything, ever."
options.then: Om frowns. "Never? Not even when I'm just curious?"

options.text: "Kind questions are fine. Just follow their lead."
options.then: Om looks relieved. "Okay. I didn't want to mess up."

options.text: "No. Ask anything. People should explain themselves."
options.then: Om grins, then hesitates. "Some questions must be too much, though?"

options.text: "Just look it up online. Asking is awkward."
options.then: Om shrugs. Reading helps, but he still feels nervous around people.

steps.why: Kind questions are welcome when the person leads. Following them is how understanding grows.

steps.prompt: Om asks: "So where's the line between curious and nosy?"

options.text: "There isn't one. Curious is always fine."
options.then: Om nods. "Okay. I'll ask everything."

options.text: "Asking about their family, basically."
options.then: Om frowns. "So everything else is okay?"

options.text: "Pushing for private stuff they didn't offer."
options.then: Om nods slowly. "So I don't push."

options.text: "Any question at all. Better never to ask."
options.then: Om sighs. "That's not very helpful."

steps.why: The line is pushing for what someone hasn't chosen to share.

steps.prompt: Om asks: "And if someone says they'd rather not answer?"

options.text: "Ask again later. They might change their mind."
options.then: Om nods. "Keep trying, then."

options.text: "Then they're probably hiding something."
options.then: Om looks thoughtful. "Hiding what, though?"

options.text: "Then say 'no problem' and drop it."
options.then: Om nods. "Easy. Just let it go."

options.text: "Then apologise a lot, so they know you meant well."
options.then: Om laughs nervously. "Wouldn't that make it weirder?"

steps.why: Respecting a 'no' warmly is part of asking gently.

scenarios.relearn: Kind, gentle questions are fine; the line is not prying or demanding.

scenarios.hook: For a class project on human diversity, you realise you don't know the respectful words to use.

steps.prompt: The project is due tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Use whatever words you've heard around
options.then: Two of the words you picked up from friends turn out to be insults.

options.text: Look up the words people use for themselves
options.then: You find a clear guide. A few words you'd heard turn out to be insults.

options.text: Leave that part out, to avoid getting it wrong
options.then: The project feels thin. The section on people is almost blank.

options.text: Borrow the words from a popular meme page
options.then: The meme words get a laugh at home, and a red mark from your teacher.

steps.why: Looking up the words people use for themselves is easy, and shows you care.

steps.prompt: During your presentation, someone asks a question using a word you've never heard. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're not sure, and ask what it means
options.then: They explain briefly. A few others look relieved that someone asked.

options.text: Nod as if you know it, and keep going
options.then: You get through it, but you still don't know the word.

options.text: Say that word sounds made-up
options.then: The room goes quiet. The person who asked looks away.

options.text: Promise to look it up later, and move on
options.then: Everyone moves on. Later, you forget to look it up.

steps.why: Not knowing is fine. Asking kindly is how anyone learns.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, a friend says all these new words are too much effort. What do you say?

options.text: "True. People are way too sensitive now."
options.then: Your friend nods. The old words stay in their vocabulary.

options.text: "You're so ignorant. Just learn them."
options.then: Your friend rolls their eyes and changes the topic.

options.text: "Then just avoid talking about people at all."
options.then: Your friend laughs. "So, never talk?"

options.text: "It's just using the words people use for themselves."
options.then: Your friend shrugs. "Okay. That's not so hard."

steps.why: Respect is simple: use people's own words, and ask when unsure.

scenarios.debrief: Not knowing a word is fine; ask kindly or look it up and use people's own words.
scenarios.relearn: When unsure of a word, ask kindly or look it up; use the words people use for themselves.

scenarios.hook: At tuition, your friend Varun says all this diversity talk is a foreign import.

steps.prompt: A few others nod along. What do you do?

options.text: Nod along to avoid an argument
options.then: Varun takes the nods as agreement and says it louder.

options.text: Call him ignorant in front of everyone
options.then: Varun reddens. "Okay, professor," he snaps.

options.text: Say "Not really" and leave it there, without a reason
options.then: Varun shrugs. "Not really how?" Nobody answers.

options.text: Gently say it's part of India's own long history
options.then: Varun looks surprised. "Really? I thought it was a Western thing."

steps.why: A calm fact, said kindly, replaces a rumour without embarrassing anyone.

steps.prompt: Varun says it must be new, since nobody talked about it before. What do you say?

options.text: It shows up across cultures and in India's old traditions
options.then: Varun goes quiet, thinking. "Huh. Nobody told me that."

options.text: Everyone online says it isn't new, so it isn't
options.then: Varun laughs. "People online say lots of things."

options.text: You just know it, and he should trust you on this one
options.then: Varun raises an eyebrow. "That's not a reason."

options.text: You'll send him a link about it sometime
options.then: Varun nods. The link never gets sent, and the idea stays.

steps.why: Pointing to history and culture gives him a reason he can actually check.

steps.prompt: Next week, Varun forwards you a video saying the same thing. What do you do?

options.text: Forward it to others for a laugh
options.then: The video spreads to three more groups.

options.text: Leave him on read
options.then: Varun sends the video to someone else instead.

options.text: Reply kindly with one calm fact about history
options.then: Varun replies: "Okay, okay. I'll think about it."

options.text: Send ten links and a long lecture
options.then: Varun sends back a single eye-roll emoji.

steps.why: Staying calm and kind helps the fact land, without a lecture.

scenarios.debrief: It isn't a foreign import; it's longstanding across cultures and India's own history.
scenarios.relearn: This diversity isn't a foreign import; it's part of India's own long history.

scenarios.hook: At break, your friends start guessing what a quiet classmate, Dhruv, 'really is'.

steps.prompt: They turn to you and ask for your guess. What do you do?

options.text: Join in with a guess of your own
options.then: Your guess gets a laugh. By lunch, it's being repeated.

options.text: Say it's not ours to guess, and change the topic
options.then: There's a pause. Someone shrugs, and the talk moves to cricket.

options.text: Stay quiet, and let them carry on guessing without you
options.then: The guessing goes on. Your silence reads as agreement.

options.text: Tell them they're all disgusting
options.then: Your friends roll their eyes. "It's just talk. Relax."

steps.why: Who someone is belongs to them. Declining to guess protects their privacy and dignity.

steps.prompt: Later, one friend says it's harmless as long as Dhruv never finds out. What do you say?

options.text: "Fair. As long as he doesn't hear."
options.then: Your friend grins. The guess gets passed along anyway.

options.text: "Even if it's harmless, it's honestly kind of boring."
options.then: Your friend shrugs. The guessing just moves elsewhere.

options.text: "I'll tell Dhruv you said it."
options.then: Your friend looks alarmed. Now the guess might reach him.

options.text: "Guesses spread, and they can really hurt him."
options.then: Your friend pauses. "I suppose it could get back to him."

steps.why: Guesses and labels about someone can harm them, even if they never hear them.

steps.prompt: That evening, someone posts a 'guess who's what' poll in the class group. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the admin to take it down, and say why
options.then: The admin deletes it. A couple of people reply "yeah, fair".

options.text: Vote, since it's anonymous anyway
options.then: The results get screenshotted and shared beyond the group.

options.text: Mute the group and ignore it
options.then: The poll runs all evening with nobody objecting.

options.text: Leave the group quietly, without saying why
options.then: The poll keeps running. Nobody knows you objected.

steps.why: Getting a labelling poll taken down stops guesses spreading about real people.

scenarios.debrief: Understanding never means labelling or guessing about any individual.
scenarios.relearn: Don't guess or label anyone; who someone is, is theirs alone.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Yusuf says he doesn't get this identity stuff, so he won't bother being polite about it.

steps.prompt: He says it while you wait for the bus. What do you say?

options.text: "You don't have to get it to be respectful."
options.then: Yusuf frowns. "Okay, but it's confusing."

options.text: "Fair. It is confusing."
options.then: Yusuf nods. "Right? Though I don't want to sound like an idiot."

options.text: "Then you're just a bigot, Yusuf."
options.then: Yusuf stiffens. "Wow. I just said I don't get it."

options.text: "Yeah, being polite is kind of fake anyway."
options.then: Yusuf laughs. "Exactly." Then, quieter: "Though I'd hate to sound dumb."

steps.why: Not understanding yet never excuses rudeness. Respect doesn't wait for full understanding.

steps.prompt: Yusuf asks how anyone learns this stuff without saying something wrong. What do you say?

options.text: "Just don't talk about it. Ever."
options.then: Yusuf shrugs. "So I stay clueless. Got it."

options.text: "Ask someone you think is like that."
options.then: Yusuf looks around. "Like who?" A guessing game has started.

options.text: "Ask kindly, listen, and say sorry if you slip."
options.then: Yusuf nods slowly. "That sounds doable."

options.text: "Watch some videos. It'll click eventually."
options.then: Yusuf saves a video and forgets it. The rudeness stays.

steps.why: Learning is fine. Asking kindly and owning slips is how anyone gets better.

steps.prompt: Next day, Yusuf makes a rude comment, then grins and says he warned you. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh, since he did warn you
options.then: Yusuf grins. The comment gets repeated at lunch.

options.text: Stop talking to him completely
options.then: Yusuf texts you, confused. Nothing about the comment gets said.

options.text: Say nothing now, and raise it some other time
options.then: Later never quite comes. Yusuf thinks it was fine.

options.text: Calmly say "That was rude" and move on
options.then: Yusuf pauses. "Okay. Yeah. That one was."

steps.why: Naming it calmly in the moment holds the respect floor while he learns.

scenarios.debrief: You can be working things out and still treat everyone with respect.
scenarios.relearn: You can be unsure and still treat people with respect; confusion never excuses rudeness.

scenarios.hook: On the bus, Tanya leans in to share her private guess about who a classmate, Aman, really is.

steps.prompt: She whispers that you mustn't tell anyone she said it. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her what made her think that
options.then: Tanya happily lists her reasons. Now you're both guessing.

options.text: Say it's not something to guess about, and leave it
options.then: Tanya shrugs. "Fine," she says, and drops it.

options.text: Pass it on to your best friend later
options.then: By evening, three people are whispering about Aman.

options.text: Listen and nod, then keep it to yourself
options.then: Tanya takes your nod as interest, and says she'll ask others too.

steps.why: Gently stopping a guess, not just keeping quiet, keeps Aman safe and respected.

steps.prompt: Next day, a friend asks if you've heard the rumour about Aman. What do you say?

options.text: "Yeah, Tanya told me too, on the bus."
options.then: Your friend's eyes light up. Now the rumour has a source.

options.text: "Is it true? What exactly did you hear?"
options.then: Your friend fills you in. The rumour grows as you talk.

options.text: "No. But who's been spreading it around?"
options.then: Your friend names three people. Now it's gossip about gossip.

options.text: "I'm not getting into guesses about people."
options.then: Your friend shrugs. "Okay, boring." The talk moves on.

steps.why: Letting a rumour stop with you keeps private things private.

steps.prompt: Aman seems quieter than usual this week. What do you do?

options.text: Treat him like always, and ask him to join you for lunch
options.then: Aman hesitates, then sits with you. He talks more by the end.

options.text: Ask him straight out if the rumour about him is true
options.then: Aman goes pale. "What rumour?"

options.text: Warn him what people are saying, so he's prepared for it
options.then: Aman's face falls. Now he's wary of everyone around him.

options.text: Keep your distance so you're not linked to the rumour
options.then: Aman notices. One more person has gone quiet around him.

steps.why: Ordinary friendliness, with no questions about the rumour, is what respect looks like.

scenarios.debrief: You can respect everyone without spreading anything private about them.
scenarios.relearn: Don't spread private guesses about people; what's private stays private.

scenarios.hook: Noor joins your class mid-term and seems unsure how she'll be treated.

steps.prompt: At lunch, Noor stands near your table holding her tiffin. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her lots of questions about herself
options.then: Noor answers politely, but looks like she's in an interview.

options.text: Wait for someone else to invite her over
options.then: Nobody does. Noor finds a seat by the window, alone.

options.text: Shift up and say "Sit here, if you like"
options.then: Noor sits down. Within minutes she's laughing at your friend's story.

options.text: Stand up and give a big welcome to the table
options.then: Everyone turns to stare. Noor smiles stiffly and sits.

steps.why: Simple, ordinary warmth makes her feel she belongs, without a spotlight.

steps.prompt: A friend whispers that Noor seems 'different' and asks what's up with her. What do you say?

options.text: "No idea. Maybe just ask her straight out."
options.then: Your friend does. Noor goes quiet and finishes her lunch fast.

options.text: "She's new. Let's just get to know her."
options.then: Your friend shrugs. "Fair. I'll say hi to her after lunch."

options.text: "Yeah, I noticed it too. Bit weird, right?"
options.then: Your friend giggles. Noor glances up, sensing something.

options.text: "Shh. Not here. Someone might hear you."
options.then: Your friend nods. You both talk about her later instead.

steps.why: Treating her like anyone else, with no guessing, is ordinary respect in action.

steps.prompt: A week on, the teacher sets a group project. What do you do?

options.text: Leave her to find a group herself
options.then: Noor ends up in a group of two.

options.text: Tell your group to be extra nice to Noor
options.then: Noor notices the special treatment and goes quiet.

options.text: Ask the teacher to put Noor somewhere
options.then: The teacher assigns her. Noor feels placed, not wanted.

options.text: Ask Noor to join your group, as you would anyone
options.then: Noor joins, and turns out to be great at slides.

steps.why: Including her the ordinary way says she belongs, no fuss needed.

steps.prompt: Later, Noor mentions her old school was rough on her. What do you say?

options.text: "Why? What happened? Who was mean to you?"
options.then: Noor hesitates. "Maybe another time."

options.text: "I'm sorry. You're welcome here."
options.then: Noor smiles. "It already feels different here."

options.text: "Well, new start. Just forget about it."
options.then: Noor nods, but it clearly still matters to her.

options.text: "Did you do something to annoy them?"
options.then: Noor stiffens. "Nothing. That's the point."

steps.why: Warm, simple acceptance, with no prying, makes a new place feel safe.

scenarios.debrief: Quiet, ordinary respect, like treating everyone the same, is understanding in action.
scenarios.relearn: Treat everyone with the same ordinary respect; quiet warmth beats a spotlight.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Gaurav insists everyone is basically the same, and difference is made up.

steps.prompt: He says it in the canteen and looks at you for backup. What do you do?

options.text: Agree with him, to keep the peace
options.then: Gaurav nods, pleased. The idea goes unchallenged.

options.text: Tell him that's the dumbest thing you've heard
options.then: Gaurav's face hardens. "Okay, genius."

options.text: Gently say people really do vary, and that's normal
options.then: Gaurav frowns. "Vary how, though?"

options.text: Say "Kind of" and quickly change the subject
options.then: Gaurav takes it as a yes and carries on.

steps.why: Saying it kindly isn't picking a fight. Variety is simply how humans are.

steps.prompt: Later, Gaurav says any differences are just people choosing to stand out. What do you say?

options.text: Nobody chooses it. People just naturally vary
options.then: Gaurav thinks. "Like height, sort of. You just are."

options.text: True. Some people choose it, to stand out
options.then: Gaurav nods. "So they could just choose not to."

options.text: It's a modern trend that started mostly online
options.then: Gaurav nods. "So it'll pass, then."

options.text: It's complicated, and you can't really explain
options.then: Gaurav shrugs. "Then maybe it is made up."

steps.why: People naturally vary in who they are and who they love. It isn't a choice or a trend.

steps.prompt: Gaurav says it'd be easier if everyone just fit in. What do you say?

options.text: "True. Fitting in keeps things simple."
options.then: Gaurav grins. "See? We agree."

options.text: "Easier for some. But nobody should have to hide."
options.then: Gaurav pauses. "Yeah. That would be rough."

options.text: "Only boring people want everyone the same."
options.then: Gaurav laughs, a bit stung. "Thanks a lot."

options.text: "Maybe. As long as nobody's actually forced to."
options.then: Gaurav nods. The pressure to fit in stays in the room.

steps.why: Expecting everyone to be the same is the myth. Room for difference is good for everyone.

scenarios.debrief: Variety is the human norm; expecting everyone to be identical is the myth.
scenarios.relearn: People really do vary; that variety is the normal human thing.

scenarios.hook: In the corridor, you overhear Pooja telling friends a scary rumour about 'what those people are like'.

steps.prompt: She turns and asks if you've heard it too. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes, and add what you've heard
options.then: The group leans in. The rumour grows another detail.

options.text: Calmly say rumours like that aren't true
options.then: Pooja blinks. "Really? Everyone's saying it."

options.text: Walk off without a word
options.then: Pooja shrugs and carries on telling it.

options.text: Tell her she's spreading hate about people
options.then: Pooja bristles. "I'm just repeating what I heard."

steps.why: Calmly saying it isn't true stops the fear, without making anyone the enemy.

steps.prompt: At lunch, Pooja tells the table her older cousin swears the rumour is true. What do you say?

options.text: "Oh. Then it's probably true."
options.then: Pooja nods, reassured. The rumour carries on.

options.text: "Your cousin sounds like an idiot."
options.then: Pooja's face tightens. "Don't talk about him like that."

options.text: "Maybe. Who really knows for sure, though?"
options.then: Pooja shrugs. The rumour seems as believable as before.

options.text: "Being older doesn't make a rumour true."
options.then: Pooja hesitates. "He does exaggerate sometimes."

steps.why: Checking facts, not who said it, is how fear gets replaced with understanding.

steps.prompt: That evening, the rumour lands in your class group as a forward. What do you do?

options.text: Forward it to another group to ask if it's true
options.then: Now two groups are reading it.

options.text: Ignore it, since someone else will deal with it
options.then: Nobody does. It gets forwarded again by morning.

options.text: Post an angry rant at whoever sent it
options.then: The chat turns into a fight. The rumour gets more attention.

options.text: Reply once, calmly, that it's false and fear-based
options.then: A few people react with a thumbs up. The forwards stop.

steps.why: One calm reply cuts the fear without fuelling a fight.

scenarios.debrief: Understanding replaces fear with facts; rumours just spread the fear.
scenarios.relearn: Don't pass on fear-based rumours; meet them with calm facts.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two moves here that cross a line into prying or labelling.

scene.text: Asking 'so what is she, really?' to gossip
Using the words people use for themselves
Reading someone's chats to guess about them
Listening when a friend shares
Letting people share at their own pace

scenarios.why: Gossip-guessing and snooping through chats are prying and labelling; the rest are respectful.
scenarios.relearn: Guessing for gossip and snooping cross the line; using people's own words, listening and patience don't.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that are slurs or insults, not respectful words.

scene.text: A mocking nickname for someone
The word a person uses for themselves
An outdated, insulting label
A plain, neutral description
Just calling them by their name

scenarios.why: A mocking nickname and an outdated insult are slurs; people's own words, neutral terms and names are respectful.
scenarios.relearn: Mocking nicknames and outdated insults are slurs; people's own words, neutral terms and their names are respectful.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths hiding among these statements about the spectrum.

scene.text: "It's a brand-new fad"
People vary naturally in who they love
"It's a foreign import"
It spans cultures and history
It's part of India's own traditions

scenarios.why: 'A new fad' and 'a foreign import' are the myths; the rest are accurate facts.
scenarios.relearn: 'New fad' and 'foreign import' are myths; natural variation across history and India is fact.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two responses that wrongly turn understanding into labelling someone.

scene.text: "So you have to pick a label now?"
"Cool, thanks for telling me."
"Let me guess what you 'really' are."
"No rush. You don't owe me anything."
"We're the same as always."

scenarios.why: Pushing a label and guessing 'what you really are' force labelling; the others respect that understanding isn't labelling.
scenarios.relearn: Pushing a label or guessing is wrong; understanding never means labelling anyone.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two fear-based rumours mixed in with the calm facts.

scene.text: "Learning about it spreads it"
Understanding replaces fear with facts
"You can catch it from people"
People are simply who they are
Knowing the facts keeps people calmer

scenarios.why: 'It spreads' and 'you can catch it' are fear-based rumours; the rest are calm, accurate facts.
scenarios.relearn: 'It spreads' and 'you can catch it' are rumours; understanding replaces fear with facts.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things here that are NOT how an ally acts.

scene.text: Joining in when others mock someone
Standing up for someone's dignity
Spreading a rumour about someone
Including a person who's left out
Using respectful words

scenarios.why: Joining mockery and spreading rumours are not allyship; backing dignity, including people and respectful words are.
scenarios.relearn: Mocking and spreading rumours aren't allyship; an ally backs dignity, includes people and uses respectful words.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two replies that make sharing weird instead of warm.

scene.text: Acting shocked and going quiet
"Thanks for trusting me."
Telling other people right after
"Nothing changes between us."
Treating them exactly the same

scenarios.why: Acting shocked and telling others betray trust; warmth, reassurance and staying the same are the respectful response.
scenarios.relearn: Shock and telling others make it weird; warmth, reassurance and staying the same are right.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two demands that don't belong in respectful curiosity.

scene.text: "Explain yourself to me right now."
"Tell me if I ever get a word wrong."
"Prove to us who you really are."
"Only share what you want to."
"I'll just ask kindly if I'm unsure."

scenarios.why: Demanding an explanation and 'prove who you are' pressure people; the rest are gentle and respect their pace.
scenarios.relearn: Demanding explanations or proof crosses a line; respectful curiosity asks gently and lets people set the pace.
